en: *Record of the Opening of the Tenets of the Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*, composed by the Śramaṇa Tanguang of the Ximing Monastery in the Capital.

Now, universal knowledge and penetrating illumination merge the ultimate and the conventional within the source of the mind; profound compassion universally pervades as he expounds the Half [Teaching].
The various schools are fully encompassed;
for indeed, through the convergence of essence and characteristics, all phenomena return to the single suchness.
Text and meaning mutually integrate, and the eight scriptural collections flow forth through the four analytical powers.
How can there be different tracks between emptiness and existence?
Why should there be divergent paths between the expansive and the concise?
One who investigates their source will find they share the same flavor as the myriad rivers.
Those who cling to its superficial branches compete to divide it into the five types of slander.
Consequently, the Hinayana drifts through the various schools of existence, causing afflictions to arise;
while the ultimate truth sinks into the void of emptiness, leading to the proliferation of contentious debates.
Yet, still driven by delusive objects, they have not yet transcended the dark path;
in vain they turn toward the true breeze and fruitlessly receive the Dharma rain.
Therefore, I, Maitreya, the one who succeeds in the place of the Buddha, extensively expound the Yoga [Śāstra].
Du [Shunzi] twice saw the gate open, realizing the single true Way;
yet, as principle encompasses all and phenomena are vast, the purport is dispersed throughout his words, which become increasingly expansive.
Consequently, former scholars grew weary of transmitting and propagating them.
Later generations grew weary of their labors in pursuing their studies;
then there appeared a Bodhisattva named Vasubandhu,
whose rank reached the pinnacle of the Three Sages and whose virtue bordered upon that of the Ten Holy Ones.
He produced a thousand treatises whose renown resounded throughout the Five Indias;
his subtle realization accorded perfectly with the Buddha’s mind, and he elegantly assisted the oral records and commentaries.
Yet, he observed that those of this degenerate age possessed meager faculties and shallow natures.
Fearing the ocean of the Dharma, they have long been separated from it;
intimidated by the mountain of its meaning, they remain forever obstructed.
Thus, they have plucked the essence from the vast scriptures.
I have condensed the essential points into this brief text and compiled this minor treatise to guide those of initial capacity,
desiring that they linger in the sublime teachings and gradually be imbued with the True Dharma.
Displaying weakness leads to ruin when returning home;
leading exhausted followers along a shortcut.
Previously, it was clarified that the hundred dharmas exist.
Subsequently, the emptiness of the two selves is revealed;
the beginning and end illuminate one another, and the conclusion and commencement reflect each other.
Once the extreme views are dispelled, the Middle Way begins to manifest.
The waves of consciousness thus subside into subtlety;
the true source thereby relies upon this to become clear and vast.
How profound is the subtle meaning of this treatise!
The title *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra* first invokes the supreme benefits of the doctrine one follows and establishes the general name of its own school.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "briefly recording names and numbers within the *Mūlavastu* (Basic Section)":
this indicates the specific basis from which the treatise arises and distinguishes it from other distinct titles used for exposition.
The Mahāyāna employs the lofty title of "Broad Conveyance";
the Hundred Dharmas manifest their names through their essential natures and numerical categories;
as the Gate of Illumination is about to open, wisdom serves as its merit.
"Śāstra" (treatise) is a designation for systematic exposition and analysis;
"basic matter" (vastu) refers to the ultimate nature of phenomena;
and "sections" (madhya) denote the topical categories of the respective parts.
This abridged record serves to suppress those verbose expressions;
these numerical categories serve to raise up this essential framework.
It is used to manifest elegant intent and established with a grand title.
Therefore, within the "Basic Section" (*Mūlavibhāga*) of the *Mahāyāna-śatadharma-vidyāmukha-śāstra*,
I shall briefly record the enumeration of names and provide an exposition of the treatise’s tenets through a fivefold analysis.
First, the clarification of the causes.
Second, it reveals the objects of cognition;
third, it clarifies the fundamental tenets;
fourth, it distinguishes the ultimate refuge.
The fivefold analysis of what has been established has two bases:
first, the basis of dependence.
Second, the causes for the sake of which.
Regarding the causes of reliance, there are furthermore five kinds.
First, reliance on the explicit teaching.
This means that the treatise is established based on the teaching of the Mahāyāna by relying on the formal presentation of the ālayavijñāna;
second, it relies on the perfect principle.
This means that the treatise is composed by relying on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to elucidate existence and emptiness through a middle-way methodological approach.
Third, it relies on the supreme object.
The fourth reliance is on sublime conduct, because one establishes the treatise by relying fully upon the five dharmas and dualistically based upon the two emptinesses,
thereby discerning all things with clarity.
Because one gives rise to profound compassion through fundamental and subsequent wisdom,
and composes treatises for the sake of propagating the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings;
fifth, it relies on the great fruit.

To fully explain the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) for the purpose of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, this treatise is composed based upon the Buddha’s complete wisdom (*pūrṇajñāna*). Regarding the causes for this, there are likewise five gates.
The first is entering the Great Dharma.
That is to say, by briefly indicating the broad and detailed principles of the doctrine,
one easily enters the Mahāyāna and becomes free from cowardice and indolence;
secondly, it gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
All phenomena are without self and are far removed from the two extremes;
this causes them to be universally penetrated so as to eliminate biased views.
Third, there is the perfect illumination of the three births.
Fourth, it causes one to advance toward realization by fully clarifying both the ultimate and conventional truths, manifesting both emptiness and existence,
so that the Middle Way may be attained and perfect illumination may arise.
It explains in detail the defiled and the pure, that which is to be abandoned and that which is realized through cultivation,
so as to ensure that correct practice is free from error;
fifth, it brings about accomplishment.
Whether partial or complete, whether transformative or actual,
the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is accomplished without deficiency;
thus ends the analysis of the causes.
To clarify the proximate conditions:
regarding the arising of the treatise, there are two kinds of objects of focus (*ālambana*).
The first is the object of focus for the composition of the treatise.
Second, the conditions for the translation and the composition of the treatise. Regarding the conditions for its composition:
since this treatise was extracted from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it is as follows.
Since the object of focus does not depart from the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
the *Yogācārabhūmivyākhyā* by the Supreme Son (Asaṅga) asks:
"What is the object of focus for this treatise that is being explained?"
This refers to how all sentient beings, from beginningless time,
have been ignorant of, doubtful about, and have held inverted and biased attachments toward the true reality within the locus of all phenomena.
Giving rise to various afflictions and initiating out-flowing karma,
one transmigrates through the five destinies and undergoes the three great sufferings.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he employs skillful means to preach various sublime dharmas concerning the true reality that abides in the middle way.
May all sentient beings understand that all phenomena are non-existent because they are empty in such and such a way,
and are not empty because they exist in such and such a way.
Thoroughly realizing that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent,
one remains far removed from doubt, inversion, and biased attachments;
by giving rise to the Middle Way, one forever severs all hindrances.
Having attained *sambodhi*, they realized the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
Six hundred years after the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*,
various sectarian schools arose in competition, and many became attached to views of existence.
They slander the Mahāyāna Dharma and destroy the True Teaching.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna realized the Stage of Supreme Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) and compiled the Mahāyāna teachings on signless emptiness.
The noble Āryadeva and other great masters composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other treatises to thoroughly elucidate the essential truth and eliminate the view of existence.
He composed the *Śataśāstra* and other works to extensively expound the Great Meaning;
consequently, sentient beings again became attached to the view of emptiness.
This continued until the beginning of the ninth century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga attained the stage of the first bhūmi;
having obtained the Samādhi of Dharma-Light and manifested great supernormal powers,
he served the Great Compassionate Honored One and requested that he expound this treatise.
There is no principle left unexplored and no phenomenon left unexhausted.
No passage remains unexplained and no meaning remains unclarified.
No doubt remains unresolved and no attachment remains unshattered.
There are no practices not cultivated and no fruits not realized.
Free from the two aforementioned views, one abides in the middle way;
by arising in the practice of the middle way, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga had a younger half-brother whose rank was that of the stage of application (*prayoga*) and whose name was Vasubandhu;
he was the twenty-second patriarch of the transmission of the Dharma treasury, as prophesied by the Buddha.
He had originally studied the Hīnayāna, becoming thoroughly proficient in various schools;
he composed five hundred treatises while concealing the Mahāyāna.
Asaṅga, taking pity on him, feigned illness to summon him and provide guidance.
It was only upon hearing the instructions on the way that he came to believe in the Mahāyāna;
he changed his course to propagate it widely and composed five hundred treatises,
as detailed in his separate biography.
This is merely a rough clarification;
because the meaning of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is extensive and its text is voluminous,
it is difficult for students to investigate, and they remain ignorant of its essential purport.
Thus, this treatise was composed as a brief summary of its essential points;
this constitutes the origin of the composition of the treatise. Regarding the circumstances of its transmission and translation:
during the Zhenguan era of the Great Tang, there was the Great Tripitaka Master, the Universal Enlightener (Pien-jue Da-shi).
His monastic name was Xuánzàng and his secular surname was Chén;
he was a native of Luòyì.
He traveled through the regions of the Five Indias to study the Tripiṭaka.
Having established his reputation and completed his work, Xuánwén returned to his native land.
Emperor Wén treated him with the etiquette due to a National Teacher (Guoshi) and issued an edict ordering him to translate sutras and treatises.
The details of his eminent legacy are fully recorded in his separate biography.
This treatise was translated by my Great Master of the Tripiṭaka at the Great Ci’en Monastery in the capital in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era.
The discussion on the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) in the second treatise is now concluded.
Next, regarding the tenets (*siddhānta*) of the third treatise:
in general, all philosophical systems do not exceed three types.
This is because of the distinctions between non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), Hīnayāna, and Mahāyāna.
Although there are ninety-six schools that the non-Buddhists follow,
they are here categorized into sixteen systems.
Therefore, the *Xiányáng lùn* (Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra) presents a summary verse stating:
"Adherence to the existence of the effect within the cause; The manifest existence of the past and future;
the self; eternalism; The view that past actions are the cause; and the harming of dharmas such as Maheśvara."
The views of finitude and infinity, pride and confusion, the view of no-cause, nihilism, emptiness,
and the conceit that one’s own doctrine is superior, pure, or auspicious— these are called the sixteen heterodox doctrines;
their establishment and refutation are explained in detail in the prose commentary of those treatises.
Now, to briefly set forth the characteristics of the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school:
first is the doctrine that the effect exists within the cause (*satkāryavāda*),
as taught by the Vārṣagaṇyas and others.
When seeking this fruit, one takes only this cause as its source,
because it arises solely from this and not from anything else;
second, the thesis is elucidated through conditions.
This refers to what is maintained by the proponents of phonology (*śabdavādin*) and others.
They assert that the essence of sound and so forth is eternal and primordially existent;
it is manifested when conditions reach it, rather than being produced from itself.
The third school, which maintains that the past and future truly exist,
is that propounded by the proponents of time (Kālavādins),
because they assert that the past and future are equally real, just like the present.
The Hīnayāna Sarvāstivādins also hold this same view.
Fourth are those who assert that the self is substantially existent;
these are the doctrines known to the followers of Paśupati and others.
Because when one perceives the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
there is a distinct perception of a "sentient being" (sattva) and so forth;
thus, [the opponent asserts] that all phenomena are eternal.
The Īśvarakāraṇikas and others assert that all phenomena,
such as atoms, are eternally permanent, because they maintain that the continuity of the characteristics of things persists through the prior and subsequent limits of time.
The thesis that the six causes are determined by past actions is that which is propounded by the Vaiśeṣikas and others:
that results such as suffering and pleasure are produced by determinate past causes.
Because they see that good and evil actions result in inverted retributions,
there is the seventh school: the doctrine of what is created by the Sovereign Lord (*Īśvara*),
as explained in the *Viṣama-śāstra*.
All intentions to perform virtuous deeds and the like are thwarted,
because worldly affairs are carried out by distinct agents. Thus,
the eight harms constitute the core of the True Dharma.
The Māṃsika Brahmin said:
"In the celestial shrines, by means of the power of mantras, one obtains rebirth in heaven through the slaughter of living beings for sacrificial offerings."
The tenets concerning the nine directions, the finite, the infinite, and so forth,
are for the sake of those who have attained worldly dhyāna,
so that they may recollect the kalpas of destruction and formation while contemplating above, below, and across.
This is because it treats as refuted the previously held views that [the self] has limits and so forth.
Tenth is the school of the "Pride of Immortality" (amara-avakīrṇaka),
which refers to the reckoning of those who are foolish and lack wisdom.
Fearing that they would lose their reputation if questioned, they did not dare answer directly;
instead, they offered a confused response based on the delusion of the "immortal heaven" (amṛtadeva).
Thus, [there arose] the eleventh thesis: that all phenomena are without cause.
He sees that a great wind suddenly arises and a violent river floods everywhere, and then he sees it subside completely, leaving everything as it was before.
This is the doctrine of annihilation after death,
established by those who propound heterodox theories.
If there were a future body, how could there be the performance of karma?
Since the self-essence is empty, both karma and its fruit do not exist.
This is the thirteenth school: the doctrine that both cause and effect are empty.
Those who have attained worldly meditative concentration and supernormal powers see that the fruits obtained from performing good and evil deeds are all distinct;
for one who enters the Brahma-conduct of meditative absorption, there is no subsequent existence.
The fourteenth is the school of false estimation of superiority;
it is the doctrine of those who adhere to the Brahminical treatises,
which asserts that the Brahmins are supreme and white in color.
Because they are of the lineage of the Brahmā-kings and practice the Brahma-faring,
there are fifteen schools that falsely reckon purity,
such as those with inferior precepts and views.
They maintain the purity of various precepts such as those regarding chickens and dogs;
they believe that bathing in the four great rivers removes sin;
and they hold sixteen speculative doctrines concerning auspiciousness.
As stated by those who discourse on calendrical calculation:
one should constantly perform offerings to the sun, moon, and stars so as not to lose the proper timing,
for the sake of accomplishing what is desired.
These sixteen kinds of adhered-to false doctrines all arise based on ignorance and erroneous reflection;
because they turn their backs on internal truth, they are all termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).
Each of the six teachers possessed these sixteen dharmas;
therefore, they are collectively said to constitute ninety-six types.
Next, there are twenty schools within the Hīnayāna tradition.
Now, one should summarize this in verse as follows:
There are twenty distinct schools; The root consists of two, and the branches eighteen.
The root comprises the Sthavira and the Mahāsāṃghika; The branches first diverge from the Mahāsāṃghika.
There is one school that speaks of the supramundane; the Kukkuṭika and Bahulaka speak of conventional reality.
Those dwelling on Mount Kukkutapāda, those of the Western Mountain, and those of the Northern Mountain are called Sthaviras;
they are known as the "Snow-Transformers" who bring forth all that exists.
The Vātsīputrīya, Dharmottarīya, Bhadrayānīya, Saṃmitīya, Kṣaṇika, Avantaka,
Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Tāmraśātīya, and Sautrāntika—
though their tenets differ, they are divided into twenty schools.
Among these, they are grouped into six schools.
First is the school that asserts both self and dharmas (I-dharma-ubhaya-satya-vāda),
namely the Vātsīputrīyas and others, who maintain that in addition to the five aggregates, twelve bases, and so forth, there exists a distinct self based upon the aggregates and other factors.
Second is the school that maintains the existence of phenomena and the non-existence of a self (dharmanairātmya).
The Sarvāstivādins and others assert that the aggregates and so forth exist as real entities throughout the three periods of time.
Because the *pudgala*— the real self— does not exist,
the Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools maintain the thesis that the three dharmas have no coming or going.
The aggregates, bases, precepts, and so forth exist in the present life;
since the past and future aggregates and so on are all non-existent,
there are four schools regarding the conventional and ultimate status of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The Saṃmitīyas and other schools maintain that the present aggregates (*skandha*) are substantially real accumulations of phenomena (*dharma*),
whereas the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) are merely conventional designations for the combination of phenomena.
This is the fifth [position] from the perspective of the True Reality school (*tattvavāda*).
The Lokottaravādins and other schools maintain that supramundane phenomena are real and not false,
whereas mundane phenomena are unreal and entirely false.
Sixth, the school that maintains the conventional designation of all phenomena (sarvadharma-prajñapti-sammatīya),
such as the Ekavyāvahārikas and others,
asserts that both mundane and supramundane phenomena are likewise entirely unreal.
However, because these are merely provisional designations lacking intrinsic nature or characteristics,
they all arise based on the teachings of the initial period;
therefore, the tenets thus adhered to constitute the Hīnayāna.
Subsequently, there are two schools within the Mahāyāna tradition.
The first is the school of Ultimate Emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*),
which includes the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Based on the teachings of non-characteristic emptiness such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
it is taught that all phenomena do not depart from the two truths.
From the perspective of conventional truth, all phenomena exist.
Even to the extent that they allow for the existence of a self and dharmas as the objects of mind,
there is no difference from the tenets of the Śrāvakayāna. However,
from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), all phenomena are empty.
This does not even establish the *vijñapti-mātratā-tathatā* (suchness of representation-only),
which is entirely different from what is taught by the *Yogācāra* school;
nevertheless, the essence of their two truths (*satya-dvaya*) is no different.
That which arises from conditions is designated as the conventional;
that very conditionality is the absence of intrinsic nature, which is called ultimate emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that the two truths are non-different in essence.
Due to delusion regarding the ultimate truth, one clings to the existence of the conventional;
even if one exerts oneself in practice, one will ultimately remain mired in saṃsāra.
By awakening to the ultimate truth, one realizes that the conventional is empty.
Therefore, one is able to realize nirvāṇa swiftly without attachment.
Thus, Prajñā is said to be the ultimate principle,
because it eliminates all marks through non-apprehension.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other such sūtras are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*),
because they do not negate the existence of the dependent and perfected natures;
those sūtras themselves declare them to be of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Because they are easy to understand for those of inferior faculties,
that which is not ultimately logical is called "provisional meaning" (neyārtha).
Second is the school of the rational, perfect, and real (nītārtha).
That is to say, based on treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Madhyāntavibhāga*,
and relying on various definitive sūtras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*,
it is taught that all phenomena are neither identical nor different in terms of the conventional and the ultimate.
It is neither existent nor empty.
This is fully analogous to the fourfold hierarchy of the conventional and the ultimate established by comparing the five dharmas in their sequential order:
first, the two truths of the unreal and the real.
The vase, the army, the forest, and so forth are empty and constitute the conventional;
the aggregates, bases, and elements, and so forth are real and constitute the ultimate.
These two—phenomena and principle—are the two truths.
The phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, being coarse, constitute the conventional (*saṃvṛti*);
the principle of the Four Noble Truths, being subtle, constitutes the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the two truths of shallow and deep, the fourfold establishment of the Four Noble Truths—being shallow—is the conventional.
The suchness of the two emptinesses is the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the four modes of expression and the two truths,
the suchness of the two emptinesses is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) accompanied by expression.
The single true dharma-realm is the ultimate truth that transcends verbal expression;
it is "not one" because it is established in contrast [to the conventional],
and it is "not different" because it has no separate essence.
Because it is grasped through delusion, it is not existent;
because its essence is not non-existent, it is not empty.
Therefore, the Profoundly Secret [Dharmadhātu] is said to be the ultimate consummation.
Because it attains the Middle Way,
the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras are considered of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*),
as they are taught from a partial perspective.
Within this, two types of doctrinal tenets are fully explained.
If one speaks of the dharma-gate of the perfect interfusion of the dharma-nature, there are then three tenets,
as in the *Qixinlun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith).
This treatise is now subsumed within the Mahāyāna as the ultimate school that is rational, perfect, and true.
The preceding exposition of the hundred dharmas reveals the existence of the dependent and the perfected natures;
the subsequent explanation of the two emptinesses reveals the non-existence of the imagined nature.
Having already departed from the two extremes and realized the Middle Way,
once the two extremes are abandoned, the Middle Way also vanishes.
The mind has nothing upon which to rely and attains absolutely nothing.
Because there is nothing attained and nothing not attained,
this is called the ultimate, perfectly realized tenet.
The exposition of the tenets is complete.
To clarify that which is taken as refuge,
there are four distinct types of refuge: refuge in the treasury,
refuge in the vehicle, refuge in time, and refuge in the divisions.
What is called the "Treasury of the Hidden" (Guizang) refers to the two treasuries and so forth.
However, as for the different types of treasuries, there are generally two kinds.
First, when distinguished according to persons, there are only two kinds.
First, the Bodhisattva Piṭaka;
second, the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
The wisdom and realization of the Pratyekabuddhas are the same as those of the Śrāvakas.
Since the teaching is not extensive, it is included within the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
"Piṭaka" (collection) means "to encompass.
It encompasses two types of persons because it respectively encompasses and benefits them in terms of the principles, practices, and fruits.
Second, they are established as the Three Piṭakas according to what they expound;
that is to say, within each of the two aforementioned [categories], there are three piṭakas.
First is the Sūtra, here translated as "Scripture" (Kīng).
It penetrates and stitches together [the teachings];
that which is explained as the study of meditative concentration (samādhi-śikṣā) accords with principle and accords with the capacities of beings, thereby gathering and benefiting others.
Second is the Vinaya, here translated as "Discipline" (tiao-fu).
The training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) which it encompasses harmonizes the three types of action (*tri-karma*),
for it restrains unwholesome conduct and brings about benefit.
Third is Abhidharma, which here is translated as "Dharma-in-Relation" (*pratisaṃvid-dharma*).
The training in wisdom it encompasses is directed toward *nirvāṇa* because it provides benefit through the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths;
this meaning is explained at length in the *Qixinlun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith).
This treatise is the *Abhidharma* within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
This is because it reveals the meaning of the bodhisattva’s principles, practices, and fruits, thereby giving rise to superior wisdom.
Regarding those who "return to the vehicle" (*yāna*),
some speak of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*:
"Because there is only the One Vehicle and no second or third,
it is sometimes spoken of as two vehicles."
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
because there is a distinction between the superior vehicle and the inferior vehicles,
some speak of three vehicles.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"For those who seek the state of a śrāvaka and so forth, he teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and the like;
or he speaks of the four vehicles."
As stated in the Śrīmālā-sūtra,
this is further augmented by the maturation of the roots of goodness of those among humans and devas who have not heard the Dharma or follow unrighteous paths; thus,
it is sometimes explained as the five vehicles.
As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*,
it further adds those whose natures in the three vehicles are indeterminate,
because upon hearing this Dharma, they give rise to the Great Mind.
However, regarding the meaning of these five vehicles, there are variations in their expansion and condensation;
thus, the explanations found in the various sūtras and śāstras differ.
This is also fully detailed as described in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*.
This present treatise is subsumed within the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and is included among the superior vehicles (agrayāna) within the two vehicles.
It explains the five dharmas and the two kinds of selflessness.
This is because it is neither the Dharma of the Two Vehicles nor a worldly dharma.
Regarding the phrase "at the time of returning," the duration of the ancient establishment of the teaching was not fixed.
That is to say, from one period up to five periods,
there is in every case no authentic basis for such claims;
fearing prolixity, I shall not enumerate them here.
Now, based on scriptural authority, the three periods of the teaching are established as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
The intended meaning of its formal exposition is as follows:
In the first period, for those of lesser faculties, he taught the doctrine of the Four Noble Truths solely from the perspective of existence to destroy the grasping at a personal self;
that is, the teachings in the four Āgamas and similar texts which affirm existence while concealing emptiness are called "provisional meaning" (neyārtha).

In the second period, for the sake of those who follow the Mahāyāna, he extensively taught the doctrine of signlessness (*animitta*) based on the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to destroy the grasping at a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-grāha*).
Thus, the teachings of emptiness in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, which conceal existence, are also of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).

Subsequently, during the third period, for the sake of all vehicles, he extensively expounded the teaching of the Middle Way regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to bring about the realization of reality.
These include the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sūtras that fully reveal both emptiness and existence; they are termed "truly definitive" (*nītārtha*).
However, these three periods are taught in a gradual sequence based on the small giving rise to the great with respect to those of indeterminate nature;
this is not the case for those of sudden-enlightenment capacity.

Second, it is like the six perfections and so forth, which are practiced in the sequence of coarse first and subtle later. Third, it is like the coarse and the subtle. For example, in the case of the six perfections and so forth, they are cultivated in the sequence of the coarse first and the subtle later.
Fourth is superiority and inferiority,
because the mind and mental factors occur in succession, with the preceding being superior and the succeeding being inferior.
Fifth is verbal expression.
Just as with the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) and so forth, although they lack the aforementioned sequence,
when they are assigned to the five preceding categories,
the mind, mental factors, matter, and non-associated formations possess a sequence of superiority and inferiority regarding their arising.

It also explains the sequence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in terms of their coarseness and subtlety; since conditioned phenomena are coarse and unconditioned phenomena are subtle,
the Hīnayāna school, following this sequence of coarseness and subtlety, takes the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*) as its starting point.
Because among all phenomena (*dharma*), form (*rūpa*) is the coarsest;
furthermore, it is because meditative practice relies on the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which is a primary gateway to the Buddha-dharma based upon the phenomenon of form;
and because it is not admitted that all phenomena are transformations of the mind.
It is not that the mind takes the mind as its primary cause.
The treatise states:
"Briefly, there are eight kinds of primary mental factors (*citta-dharma*). Kai says:
Next, the fourth section follows, which extensively analyzes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The analysis of the first five phenomena is divided into five parts.
Within the first category, the phenomena of the initial mind, it is further divided into two.
First the number is indicated, and subsequently the items are distinguished and enumerated;
this is the first [part].
That is to say, regarding these mental factors (*cittadharma*), there are differing explanations in various teachings.
In both the Hīnayāna and within the Mahāyāna,
the systems of conventional discourse speak only of the first six [consciousnesses],
and even there, they do not admit that they arise simultaneously in a single moment.
Therefore, in accordance with whatever single consciousness arises in the present,
the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other texts distinguish between the defiled and pure aspects of the ālayavijñāna, thereby teaching that there are nine consciousnesses. Alternatively,
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* establishes eleven consciousnesses based on the triad of sense faculties, objects, and consciousnesses associated with the first six consciousnesses.
In scriptures such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, seven names are established for the ālayavijñāna based on its general and specific states;
however, the position of "one consciousness" (*ekavijñānavāda*) taught in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not distinguish the former six.
However, they are generally spoken of as three;
such teachings as these occur in many places throughout the scriptures.
Now, speaking of their essential nature, there are only eight kinds.
Because the various teachings differ in length according to their expansion or contraction, the treatise states:

"First, eye-consciousness; second, ear-consciousness; third, nose-consciousness; fourth, tongue-consciousness; fifth, body-consciousness; sixth, mental consciousness; seventh, manas-consciousness; eighth, ālaya-vijñāna. This is the expanded [presentation].
This is the enumeration. Now,
regarding these eight consciousnesses, which constitute the great core of the sacred teachings,
the masters of former generations have all provided extensive expositions on their fundamental categories.
Now, opening this concise treatise, it would be inappropriate for the text to be overly prolix;
therefore, I shall clarify the essential points through a tenfold classification.
First: explaining the names to reveal the essence.
Second, association with mental factors;
third, the objective referent;
fourth, the various modes of activity.
Fifth, the similarities and differences among the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
sixth, the existence or non-existence of the various feelings (*vedanā*);
seventh, the number of their respective bases (*āśraya*).
Eighth, there is the deficiency regarding the object of cognition;
ninth, the distinction between the perfuming agent and that which is perfumed;
tenth, the difference in essence between annihilation and permanence.
Although these ten thematic categories are discussed in various treatises,
they are most complete and clear in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. Therefore,
I shall now explain them primarily based on the text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
First, regarding the manifestation of the essence of the names, there are four propositions.
Some teachings state that general and specific names are interchangeable;
for instance, although the eight [consciousnesses] are generally termed "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Based on the predominance of their respective characteristics, the distinctions between mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are explained.
The eighth [consciousness] is called "mind" (*citta*) because it accumulates the seeds of all phenomena and gives rise to all phenomena.
The seventh is called *manas* (mind),
because its nature is to deliberate with discernment and to take the form of a self.
The preceding six are called *vijñāna* (consciousness).
Because its perception of objects is coarse and superior to that of other consciousnesses,
this [consciousness] is designated by this specific name within the general category; or,
according to some teachings, it is given this specific name among the various [types of consciousness].

Furthermore, although the first six consciousnesses are individually termed "consciousness," they each receive three distinct names based on their respective functions regarding the sense faculties and objects;
it is only by depending upon the sense faculties that they are designated as "eye-consciousness" and so forth.
Because they are the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth, [terms such as] "eye-consciousness" are analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Because names and forms are established in accordance with their respective objects, [terms such as] "name-and-form-consciousness" and so forth are analyzed according to the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound; since consciousness possesses form, they are all analyzed according to the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Names such as "seeing-consciousness" (*darśana-vijñāna*) are established according to their function;
since seeing is itself consciousness, these are both *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds.
Now, this treatise explains that while names are established according to the sense organs (*indriya*), the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is not established according to the objects (*viṣaya*).
The name is established according to the faculty because it possesses five meanings.
These five are: basis (*āśraya*), origination (*samutthāna*), belonging (*sambandha*), assistance (*anugraha*), and similarity to the faculty (*tulyārthatva*).
First, because it is consciousness that relies upon the eye, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
It must depend on the unimpaired faculty for visual consciousness to arise;
even when a visible form is present, one who is blind does not see it.
Because it is the consciousness produced by both eyes, it is called "visual consciousness."
Just as when a disease impairs the eye-consciousness, one sees everything as yellow;
this is not because the object (color) has degenerated such that the consciousness erroneously perceives it.
Because the consciousness belongs to the eye, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
The seed of visual consciousness arises following the seed of the eye;
it does not arise from the seed of form, for visual consciousness is so named because it assists the eye. Thus, it is called "eye-consciousness."
Because consciousness, in conjunction with the sense faculty, experiences [objects],
and because the impairment or benefit of the faculty does not arise from the object-form (rūpa),
it is called "eye-consciousness" (cakṣurvijñāna) because its consciousness is like that of the eye.
Just as the sense-faculties are definitely sentient beings because they possess the capacity for illumination,
form is not determinate in this regard; since it is so for the visual consciousness,
it is likewise for the others.
The other consciousnesses are to be understood by analogy.
They are designated according to their respective objects; although this accords with the general meaning of "consciousness," [it does not apply to the storehouse consciousness].
This is spoken only with respect to the state where the five sense faculties have not yet attained mastery.
In the state of mastery, however, the faculties function interchangeably;
a single faculty gives rise to consciousness that perceives all objects.
This would result in the error of the six consciousnesses being confused with one another.
One should understand that the same applies to designating names according to their respective functions;
however, as long as the specific sense organs they follow are taken into account, there will be no confusion.
Furthermore, the sixth consciousness is given a distinct name in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, called the "discriminating consciousness of phenomena" (*vicitravastuvijñaptivijñāna*),
because it discriminates between various internal and external phenomena.
In the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda Śāstra*), it is termed the "separating consciousness" (*prativijñaptivijñāna*).
Because it separately relies upon the six sense organs to apprehend the six objects,
its seventh consciousness is given the general and specific name *manas*;
this is translated here as "mind" (*yi*).
Because its nature and characteristic consist in constant and thorough deliberation,
how does this differ from the sixth consciousness?
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, just like the name "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*).
Because consciousness is identical to the mind (*manas*),
it is a dependent compound (*tatpuruṣa*), as in the term "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Because consciousness is distinct from the mind, [it is a possessive compound].
This manas has three further distinct names:
first, when associated with the view of a personal self (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi), it is called the afflicted manas (kliṣṭa-manas);
second, when associated with the view of a phenomenal self (dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi), it is called the obscured manas (nivṛta-manas).
The state associated with the wisdom of the equality of the three [spheres] is called the purified mind (*manas*).

This initially pervades the mental continuum of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the stage of the contaminated mind of those in training (*śaikṣa*) among the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and a certain class of bodhisattvas prior to the seventh bhūmi.
Taking that ālayavijñāna as its object, it gives rise to the view of a personal self (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi).

Subsequently, it persists throughout the mental continuums of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas during those stages when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna) has not yet manifested.
Taking that maturation-consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātmadṛṣṭi*).

Subsequently, throughout the continuum of all Tathāgatas, during the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), at the stage where the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) is manifest before one.
Taking that stainless consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the Wisdom of Equality.
Regarding the specific names of this eighth consciousness,
there are three distinct names based on its different stages.
It is named *ālaya*, which is translated as "storehouse" (*zàng*).
This is because it carries the meanings of being that which stores, that which is stored within, and that which is clung to.
That is to say, the preceding seven consciousnesses all arise from seeds [within it].
The essential nature and characteristics of cause and effect cannot be definitively differentiated;
thus, this very seed is taken as the eighth consciousness,
and all seven consciousnesses are subsumed within this consciousness.
It is called "the storehouse" because it gathers and conceals all phenomena within its own substance.
The seeds of the various consciousnesses are perfumed by the seven consciousnesses;
they are their residual impressions and are not separate from the seven consciousnesses.
Since it takes up seeds as its eighth consciousness,
and these seeds are subsumed within the preceding seven consciousnesses,
it is called "that which is stored" (*ālaya*) because it stores its own essence among all phenomena.
Since beginningless time, it has continued spontaneously,
appearing as if it were a single entity and permanent;
because it possesses the characteristic of a real self, the seventh consciousness constantly grasps it as the self.
It is called "appropriated" (ālaya) because it is comprised by the view of self;
"appropriation" (ālaya) refers to its functional activity,
while "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to its essential substance.
"Storehouse" (*ālaya*) is an *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the storehouse of consciousness.
This name applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*),
and not to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) or non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas.

Because it has the sense of being a repository (*ālaya*) for the grasping of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*), the name "ālayavijñāna" is explained as being based on this grasping; this is because the former two meanings apply throughout the subsequent stages.
For this reason, this name carries the most significant fault.
Because it is abandoned first, it is specifically mentioned here.
Second is the *vipāka*,
which is called the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness).
That is to say, the essential nature of this consciousness is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
it is that which can project the fruits of birth within the realms of existence and destinies— whether wholesome or unwholesome—
and is thus termed "maturation" (*vipāka*).
They ripen at different times;
they ripen through transformation;
they ripen as different types.
Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called "ripening" (*vipāka*).
If the first two meanings alone were sufficient to be termed "ripening," then the first seven consciousnesses and so forth would also receive this name.
The cause and the fruit differ in time;
it is through the transformation of the cause that the fruit finally ripens,
as this principle applies universally.
Regarding the designation "vipāka" (maturation) based on the latter meaning,
only the eighth consciousness alone receives this name,
because it is the neutral fruit induced by wholesome and unwholesome causes.
The meaning of "maturation as a different class" does not apply to other consciousnesses;
thus, while the sense of "difference" applies generally to both cause and effect,
"maturation" pertains exclusively to the fruit.
There are two kinds of fruition:
the seed and the manifestation.
If they were different, it would belong to the cause; thus, it is the maturation of that which is different.
If "transformation" (vipāka) refers to something distinct from its fruit, then it is simply maturation (pakti).
Maturation is the maturation of consciousness; this maturation pertains to the manifest (pravṛtti), while the maturation of the maturing consciousness pertains to the seed (bīja).
Therefore, the other evolving consciousnesses do not receive this name.
This name applies only to the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and the various bodhisattva stages;
it does not apply to the stage of the Tathāgata, because there still exist dharmas that are matured (*vipāka*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is called the *amala* (stainless),
which is the name for the immaculate consciousness (*vimala-vijñāna*),
because it is the basis for all the most extremely pure, vast, and sublime untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
"Stainless" (*vimala*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "stainless consciousness.
This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata.
In the stages of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there exist contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) that are susceptible to being perfumed (*bhāvya*).
Because the eighth consciousness has not yet attained complete purity,
these are all specific names within the category of "specific. Alternatively,
certain teachings establish a general name that encompasses the specific.
The first six consciousnesses are collectively termed "experiential," because they experience the six sense objects and thereby produce the fruit of suffering;
in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, they are called "arising consciousnesses."
Because they arise from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
if the seventh [consciousness] is included, they are collectively termed *pravṛttivijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses),
as they evolve intermittently during the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) and other stages.
If the eighth consciousness is subsumed under the first three names and possesses four types of designations across all stages,
it may be called the "root consciousness" (mūlavijñāna).
Because it is the fundamental source from which the various phenomena of defilement and purity of the preceding seven consciousnesses arise,
it is called *ādāna* (appropriation). Alternatively,
it is so named because it grasps and maintains the seeds and the material sense organs, preventing them from perishing.
It is also called the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*),
because it serves as the support for all phenomena that are known, whether defiled or pure.
It is also called the "seed-consciousness" (*bījavijñāna*).
Because it is able to universally sustain all seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms,
these are all general names within the specific [categories].
Alternatively, there are teachings that speak of general names within the general [categories].
This means that the aforementioned specific and general names are further subsumed under the general name "mind" (citta), "consciousness" (vijñāna), and "mentality" (manas).
Regarding the aforementioned general sense, it is designated by the general name "mind."
Because it takes objects as its focus and arises through association with all consciousnesses,
the preceding heading states:
There are eight mental factors.
Alternatively, all [eight] meanings may be termed "mind" (manas),
because they all possess the sense of being the basis for production.
Therefore, within the category of bases (*āyatana*), they are collectively termed the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
Alternatively, these various meanings are collectively termed consciousness (*vijñāna*),
because all are capable of discerning the characteristics of their respective objects.
Therefore, within the five aggregates, all are subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*),
and thus they are all designated as "consciousness" in the treatise's enumeration.
The Hīnayāna schools generally rely upon the eye and other faculties across the three periods of time.
That which is future is called "mind" (citta) because it has the sense of accumulation;
that which enters the present is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Because it is capable of discerning [objects],
the past [consciousness] is called "mind" (manas);
because it serves as the guiding and introductory support (āśraya).
Whenever a mind arises, it must necessarily be associated with mental factors (caitta).
These arise together with the mind according to its specific nature;
that is to say, the natures of the eight consciousnesses are wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, or unobscured-neutral.
That which is beneficial and conducive to both this world and other worlds is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Although the pleasant fruits of humans and devas are conducive to benefit in this world, they are not so in other worlds;
therefore, they are not termed "wholesome."
They are called unwholesome because they cause harm and opposition in both this world and other worlds.
Although the bitter fruits of the miserable realms (durgati) cause harm in this world, they do not do so in other worlds;
therefore, they are not unwholesome.
It is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it cannot be defined in terms of wholesome or unwholesome matters that bring benefit or harm.
It is called "obscured" (*nivṛta*) because its nature is defiled, capable of veiling the mind and obstructing the Noble Path.
Because it is not defiled, it cannot obscure the mind nor obstruct the noble path; therefore, it is called "unobscured.
The eighth consciousness is exclusively unobscured-neutral, because this consciousness is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
If the ripening [consciousness] were either wholesome or defiled,
the processes of saṃsāra and its cessation would be impossible.
Furthermore, this consciousness is the basis for both the wholesome and the defiled.
Furthermore, because the wholesome and the defiled are mutually contradictory,
this consciousness should not serve as the substratum for both;
moreover, this consciousness is by nature that which is perfumed (*bhāvyatva*).
If that which is wholesome or defiled were like an extremely fragrant or foul odor, it should not be susceptible to perfuming;
since there would be nothing to be perfumed, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity would fail to be established.
Thus, one must accept that greed and the like are exclusively wholesome or defiled.
Therefore, it is definitely not associated with this consciousness.

Furthermore, the four [mental factors] such as regret (*kaukṛtya*), which are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and have specific objects (*viśaya-viśeṣa*), are also not associated with it because they are intermittent.
As for the five [mental factors] with specific objects, they take various distinct objects.
That is to say, desire functions by turning toward objects of one's longing;
this consciousness functions spontaneously without such longing, and its resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) maintains a determined object.
This consciousness is obscure and lacks any firm retention.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) functions by clearly recollecting things previously experienced;
this consciousness (*vijñāna*), being dull and inferior, cannot clearly recollect.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is able to cause the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object.
This consciousness spontaneously perceives distinct objects moment by moment,
whereas wisdom functions only by discerning qualities and other such phenomena;
this consciousness is subtle and indistinct, and thus incapable of discernment.
Therefore, these do not associate with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*).

The five factors—contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—are universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta-dharma*). Thus, they necessarily accompany every state of mind.
If these five [mental factors] are absent, the mind necessarily does not arise;
for without contact, feeling, and so forth, it is not designated as "mind.
Their universal characteristics will be explained in detail later.
The seventh is exclusively obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Its nature is defiled because it obstructs the Noble Path and obscures one’s own mind; thus, it is called "obscured.
Because certain internal attachments do not give rise to benefit or harm in this life or future lives, it is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, it is associated with only eighteen mental factors:
namely, the five beginning with contact;
from among the specific object-conditions, wisdom (*prajñā*), self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*).
The eight secondary afflictions (upakleśas) are necessarily associated with the mental faculty and with the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika),
because one who clings to a self or to phenomena must necessarily possess discernment (prajñā).
Fools are deluded regarding the characteristic of self because they fail to understand non-self;
they falsely conceptualize and speculate upon phenomena that are not the self;
and they give rise to arrogance by relying on the self they have grasped.
Because it is deeply attached to the self as it is grasped,
and because the eight secondary afflictions (upakleśa) universally defile the mind,
why does this consciousness lack other mental factors?
Because the view of self arises constantly without exception;
because there cannot be two types of wisdom within a single moment of mind;
and because the functions and meanings of wisdom and the view of self are distinct.
Because one sees with certainty and is free from hesitation;
because one does not feel hatred toward the "self" grasped by craving;
and because one constantly takes composite objects as one's focus, being free from longing.
Because it constantly takes a fixed object as its focus without sustained apprehension;
because it constantly takes a present object as its focus without memory;
and because it takes distinct objects moment by moment without single-minded concentration.
The wholesome is exclusively pure;
this [state] is defiled.
The ten minor [afflictions] are coarse and violent.
Because this is subtle,
the middle two are unwholesome;
because this is indeterminate, [the others are so].
Because [the meditative state] always takes a fixed object as its condition and does not involve remorse for what was done previously;
whereas sleep depends on external conditions,
this [state] arises from within.
Because vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) belong to the same category of being coarse and subtle respectively,
there are only eighteen mental factors associated [with them].
The sixth consciousness, the manovijñāna, however, is associated with all categories [of mental factors].
It possesses various modes of conceptualization that operate through internal and external gates,
for it can be definitively characterized as either harmful or beneficial; thus,
although the defilements it gives rise to may be temporarily suppressed by meditative concentration, they remain present.
The nature [of the mind] is neither diminished nor enhanced, because it does not obstruct the Noble Path.
The mind that constitutes the maturation fruit (vipākaphala) induced by completing karma (pūrṇakarma) is not defiled,
because it does not obstruct the Path.
Therefore, it is compatible with all mental factors (*caitta*).
Although they do not all arise simultaneously,
whichever of the three natures (*tri-śvabhāva*) arises, it is associated with those very factors.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, operate according to external objects;
they also share the same four mental natures as the mental consciousness,
because they lack the functions of constructive (abhinirūpaṇā) and recollective (anusmaraṇa) discrimination.
It is associated with only thirty-four mental factors:
namely, the five universal factors, the five object-specific factors,
the eleven wholesome factors, and the three root afflictions.
The middle two [categories] consist of eighty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Because they are universally associated with the mind, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth,
and because they can apprehend various objects in a subtle and inferior manner.
Furthermore, because they overturn various wholesome dharmas;
because they consist of the unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion;
and because lack of shame and lack of dread are universally unwholesome.
Since restlessness and the other seven [mental factors] pervade all defiled minds,
why do the remaining mental factors not correspond with them?
It is because pride and the like arise through processes such as deliberation (*tulanā*).
Because the small and the ten [factors] are coarse and violent, while this [state] is subtle and weak;
because regret and sleep are not among the five factors;
and because vitarka and vicāra are the unique (asādhāraṇa) dharmas of the mind.
This is explained according to the three natures during the stage of the cause;
if it pertains to the stage of the fruit, it is entirely untainted and wholesome,
and is associated with twenty-one mental factors.
The five omnipresent mental factors, the five object-specific mental factors,
and the eleven wholesome mental factors are always associated with all states of mind;
for they constantly delight in realizing and cognizing the objects under observation.
Because he constantly maintains mental focus upon the objects of observation;
because he constantly and clearly recollects objects previously experienced;
and because the Blessed One possesses no state of mind that is not concentrated.
Because they constantly exercise discernment regarding all phenomena;
because they are always associated with supreme pure faith and so forth;
and because they are free from defilement and free from distraction.
It is not associated with indeterminate mental factors and so forth;
since it is associated with these various mental factors,
its objects of perception likewise vary in breadth and narrowness.
Regarding the five consciousnesses within the causal stage, they take as their objects only the five sense-objects— form and so forth— whether provisional or real,
as will be explained below. Furthermore,
there are two theories concerning the objects of these five consciousnesses.
Some say that the five consciousnesses take only real objects as their conditions,
because they arise spontaneously without depending on names and phrases,
and because they arise in dependence upon these other sense organs and objects.
Other derivative forms, such as length and so forth,
must depend upon names and expressions as well as other factors for their arising; therefore,
one does not take these derivative forms, such as length, as objects of perception.
Some say that the five consciousnesses also take conceptual objects as their domain;
since qualities such as long and short are also subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*),
it is not contrary to reason for visual consciousness to take them as its object.
However, when the mind conditions the provisional, it conditions the real;
when it conditions the real, it does not condition the provisional.
The real does not depend upon the provisional.
Because it relies on the real as a basis for its designation,
the sixth consciousness conditions all objects and possesses all forms of discrimination,
such as the seven types and the three types.
Because it is the most preeminent among the consciousnesses that discern objects,
if the seventh consciousness takes only the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its object, perceiving it as the self,
and does not take its image-portion (nimitta-bhāga) as its object.
The seeds within consciousness and its associated mental factors are taken as "mine.
This is because the grasping at "I" and "mine" do not arise simultaneously;
rather, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) associated with this consciousness arises spontaneously, as a single class, and continues in a constant succession.
Because it is impossible for a separate grasping at "mine" (mamakāra) to arise [in relation to this consciousness].
Wherever it is said that one grasps at "self" and "mine," it means that one grasps this consciousness as the "self of the self."
Therefore, regarding the single meaning of "seeing," two terms are spoken.
Although the eighth consciousness is subtle such that both its object-condition (*ālambana*) and its mode of activity (*ākāra*) are unknowable,
it arises as a self-substance through the power of causes and conditions.
Internally, it transforms the seeds and the appropriated material sense-faculties;
externally, it transforms the appearance of the container world that serves as its basis.
It takes these very transformations as its own objects of perception and cognitive modes.
This is because one arises by relying upon it.

If there are those in the form realm who possess all three types of objects of cognition, while in the formless realm there are only those who take as their objects of cognition the seeds and the unchanging mind and so forth; [then...]
The transformations of tainted consciousness are, in brief, of two kinds:
first, those that transform due to the power of causes and conditions;
second, those that transform due to the power of conceptual discrimination.
Initially, it necessarily has a functional utility;
subsequently, it serves merely as an object.
The forms and so forth transformed by the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) necessarily possess actual utility, as they are transformed solely in accordance with causes and conditions.
If the transformed mind and so forth were rendered useless because the object-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the mind and so forth cannot take them as objects,
then their actual utility must arise separately from this [transformation].
Therefore, the eighth consciousness does not take mind and its associates as its objects.
However, if this consciousness takes the seeds of the seven consciousnesses as its objects,
it may also be said to "take them as objects" by subsuming the derivative into the fundamental.
However, according to their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), they lack the sense of having an object.
All of these [statements] are explained based on the stage of being with outflows (*sāsrava*).
In the stage without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are associated with the four wisdoms (*jñāna*).
It universally takes all objects, both ultimate and conventional, as its cognitive domain;
otherwise, the fruit of Buddhahood would not be omniscient.
All these objective appearances are transformations of one's own mind.
In reality, they are not separate from the mind,
for they are divisions of the mind.
Furthermore, these divisions of the mind are, in total, of four kinds.
First is the object-aspect (nimittabhāga);
second is the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga);
third is the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga).
Fourth is the self-cognizing portion (svasaṃvittibhāga).
This means that when the substance of any contaminated consciousness arises,
it always manifests in the likeness of both the perceived object and the perceiving subject.
It should be understood that the associated mental factors are likewise so.
That which resembles the aspect of the object is called the *nimittabhāga* (image-part);
that which resembles the aspect of the subject is called the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part).
If mind and mental factors lacked the characteristic of having an object of cognition,
they would either be unable to cognize their respective objects,
or each one would be able to cognize all things.
Because its own object is like others,
and others are like it; for if mind and mental factors lacked the characteristic of being able to cognize, [they would not function as objects].
It should not be able to take an object,
like space and so forth;
or else, space and so forth would also be capable of taking an object.
Therefore, one should know that there must necessarily be two parts:
the image-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga). The image-part is the object-condition (ālambana), while the seeing-part is termed the mode-of-apprehension (ākāra).
The mutual perception [of the aspects] must necessarily have a self-substance as its basis;
this very self-substance is termed the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
If this were non-existent, there would be no self-verifying portion.
One should not be able to recollect the mind and mental factors themselves,
because one cannot recollect them in the same way as an object never previously experienced; furthermore,
the [subjective] aspect (nimittabhāga) and the [objective] aspect (darśanabhāga) would lack a substantial basis.
Because there would otherwise be no object of cognition, no means of cognition, and no result of cognition,
we know that this self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) must necessarily exist.
Since the portions of the mind are of the same nature, they must necessarily verify one another.
If there were no fourth [cognition], who would verify the third? Therefore, there must further be a self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
This is the fruit of the third [self-cognizing] portion, because all means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) necessarily possess a fruit.
The seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) should not be regarded as the third fruit,
because the seeing-portion is sometimes subsumed under non-valid cognition (apramāṇa),
whereas that which realizes its own essence must necessarily be direct perception (pratyakṣa).
If that were so, one would have to establish a fifth member, which would lead to the fault of infinite regress.
The answer is: it is simply the third member that serves as a retroactive proof for the fourth.
This is because they are all established through the testimony of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The first two are external;
the latter two are internal.
Initially, it is solely the object of cognition;
subsequently, it pervades both [subject and object].
Neither identical nor separate, it is never apart from the mind.
The objects of perception are fully established, and there is no fault of infinite regress.
These four parts of the contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) are all pervasive;
as for uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*), their presence or absence is not fixed.
This means that the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) perceives with an aspect (sākāra) but lacks an object (anālambana).
Since true wisdom must necessarily possess the factor of seeing (darśana-bhāga),
if it lacked this factor of seeing, it would be incapable of taking an object.
It would be more appropriate to describe it as the wisdom that takes suchness as its object;
for one must not claim that the nature of suchness itself is also a subjective perceiver.
Therefore, one must admit that this meditative concentration possesses a seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*).
Although there is the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga), it is without conceptualization (vikalpa);
this is because it is said that while it apprehends the signless (animitta), it does not apprehend signs.
Although there is no image-part (nimitta-bhāga), this [seeing-part] can still be so described.
Because it arises bearing the characteristic of suchness and does not depart from suchness;
just as when the self-witnessing portion (svasaṃvittibhāga) takes the seeing portion (darśanabhāga) as its object,
it takes it as an object without undergoing transformation.
This case should also be understood in the same way:
that which perceives through transformation does not constitute direct realization,
because it possesses the appearance of an object, just like subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
If it is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), both parts are present;
this is because this category of wisdom is said to possess conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
It is said that this reflection is merely similar to the appearance of *tathatā*.
Because they do not perceive the true characteristic of suchness,
they differentiate the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena; yet,
observing all sentient beings, they preach the Dharma for their sake.
Although the two types of wisdom in the latter two parts both function as objects of cognition,
they differ in whether or not they possess the activity of taking [objects] as their conditions.
That is to say, fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) does not take anything as its object-condition.
If the subsequently attained wisdom possesses the function of having an objective aspect,
it is because the two functions— having an aspect and being aspectless— are distinct.
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the four divisions.
One should understand that the various characteristics of the objects of consciousness previously described are precisely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of consciousness;
because they are portions of the mind, they are neither identical to nor separate from the mind.
All minds and mental factors, being free from [the notion of] a self, possess four aspects;
however, there are distinctions regarding that which cognizes the object.
Specifically, the cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the eight consciousnesses is generally of three types.
The first is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means being present before one;
"perception" (*pramāṇa*) means the act of measuring or determining.
That is to say, one clearly perceives the manifest forms and so forth,
understanding them as non-erroneous characteristics;
free from all categories of verbal expression and conceptual discrimination, they are illuminated with mirror-like clarity.
Therefore, it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Direct" (*pratyakṣa*) is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*).
Second is inference (*anumāna*).
"Comparison" (anumāna) refers to drawing an analogy; its meaning is the same as that of "inference" (pramāṇa) mentioned previously.
It refers to [the cognition] regarding forms and so forth that are not present before one.
When, by means of various signs, correct knowledge arises regarding the object of observation—
such as the realization that there is a "great" [self] or that things are impermanent and so forth—
this is called inference (*anumāna*).
"Comparison" (upamāna) is both the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the act of cognizing;
it is thus explained as a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Third is "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*), which refers to an object that is not clearly and vividly manifest to direct perception.
Nor can it be inferred through various conditions;
since the substance of the object does not truly exist, it cannot be measured.
One gives rise to mental measurement toward that which is beyond measurement.
Therefore, it is called "non-means of valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*). Thus, it does not constitute one of the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*).
However, these three means of valid cognition are all discussed in relation to the mind.
This is not stated in terms of the object;
for [the latter] is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, among the eight consciousnesses, the five sensory consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because it lacks constructive (abhinirūpaṇā) and recollective (anusmaraṇa) conceptualization and operates spontaneously toward its objects,
if the manas-consciousness were exclusively non-valid cognition (apramāṇa), [it would not function as such].
Because the eighth consciousness is clung to as self and phenomena,
it falsely discriminates that which is not self or phenomena;
whereas the sixth consciousness can generally possess all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because it can thoroughly cognize all objects— including all conceptual constructions such as the "nature of self" (svabhāva) and so forth—
among the four parts [of consciousness], the first part, the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), is exclusively the object of cognition (*prameya*).
The latter three [aspects] each pertain to two [of the three cognitions];
the subsequent [aspect], the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), pertains to all three cognitions;
and the final two parts are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The realization of the self-nature must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is explained with reference to the eight consciousnesses during the stage of the cause;
however, if one relies on the stage of the fruit, there are also distinctions.
That is to say, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is entirely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), however, also encompasses all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because it takes as its objects all phenomena, whether their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Once there is a corresponding apprehension of the object through measurement, one experiences what is favorable or unfavorable.
This characteristic of experience is briefly of three kinds.
The experience of an unfavorable object that oppresses the body and mind is called the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).
The experience of a favorable object that brings gratification to body and mind is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
The experience of a neutral object that is neither oppressive nor gratifying to body and mind is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*).
Within suffering and pleasure, each is further divided into two, namely:
suffering, grief, joy, and pleasure, because they differ from one another;
and because their respective characteristics of afflicting or gladdening the body and mind are distinct.
Because of the distinction between the non-conceptual and the conceptual,
and because of the difference between the extremely heavy and the slight,
there is no division into two for that which is neither painful nor pleasant.
Because they are neither exclusively pleasant nor exclusively delightful, because their characteristics are not different,
because they are non-conceptual, and because they function with equanimity,
all pleasant and delightful sensations associated with the five consciousnesses are always termed "pleasure" (sukha).
That which is associated with the mental consciousness is called joy (*prīti*) and called pleasure (*sukha*).
If it occurs in the desire realm or in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first two dhyānas, it is called joy,
because it merely gladdens the mind.
If one is in the fundamental stages of the first or second dhyāna, it is called pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*),
because they gladden both body and mind;
in the fundamental stage of the third dhyāna, it is called pleasure.
Because Śāntamati places particular emphasis on non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*),
all painful sensations associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are always termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*).
Those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are termed "grief" (*daurmanasya*) or "suffering."
Among humans and devas, it is always termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*),
because although there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it is not particularly intense.
Among animals and hungry ghosts, it is termed both "sorrow" and "suffering" (*duḥkha*).
Because mixed sensations and pure sensations have degrees of intensity,
those in the hells are designated as "suffering" alone; for there,
the pure sensation is exclusively intense and devoid of discrimination.
Apart from these stages, that which is neither painful nor pleasant—
whether pertaining to the body or the mind— is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Alternatively,
it is termed equanimity throughout the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*) of the fourth dhyāna, as well as in all stages above them.
Because it proceeds with equanimity;
because it is the stage of immovability, free from the experience of change;
