and because there is no distinction between body and mind.
Thus, one should know that the six consciousnesses and the three feelings can coexist;
however, in the state of mastery, there are only joy, pleasure, and equanimity,
because all Buddhas have already severed the factors of suffering and sorrow.
If the seventh consciousness has, from beginningless time, functioned spontaneously as a single category,
taking the internal as its object and grasping it as a self without ever undergoing change,
then it would not arise simultaneously with fluctuating feelings (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*), because such feelings involve alteration.
That eighth consciousness is extremely indistinct;
it cannot differentiate between the characteristics of favorable or unfavorable objects,
because it evolves as a subtle, uniform, and continuous stream.
Therefore, they are all associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Even when in the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), they are associated only with equanimity,
because they function spontaneously and perpetually in a state of equilibrium.
Although these various meanings depend upon the mind and mental factors,
the mind and mental factors themselves all possess a basis;
furthermore, there are three general types of such bases.
First is the causal-condition support (hetu-pratyaya-āśraya), namely one's own seeds;
all conditioned phenomena depend upon this support.
Because nothing can arise apart from its own causes and conditions;
however, while the cause and effect of a seed within its own category do not coexist,
the arising of the seed and the manifestation [of the fruit] are necessarily simultaneous.
Just as bundles of reeds stand together by supporting one another,
so too the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors must each have their own distinct seeds as their basis.
Second is the basis of the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
which refers to the six internal bases (*āyatana*).
All minds and mental factors depend upon these as their support.
Because they would necessarily fail to function if separated from their co-existent faculties,
among these, the five consciousnesses have four bases:
namely, the five material sense-faculties and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
Because if even one of these is lacking, [the consciousness] will certainly not arise;
because their objects are identical while their functions of discriminating between defilement and purity and their fundamental supports are different;
and because the supported basis for the sixth mental consciousness consists of only two types.
This refers to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
for if either one is missing, the other necessarily does not arise,
and because their respective fundamental supports (āśraya) are distinct and not shared.
If the manas-consciousness has a simultaneous support, it has only one kind,
namely the ālayavijñāna;
for if the store-consciousness were absent, the manas would certainly not function.
The ālayavijñāna also has one type of simultaneous support,
namely the manas-vijñāna;
for if the defiled manas were absent, it would certainly not function.
Regarding the statement that the ten [consciousnesses], such as eye-consciousness, have conditions (*pratyaya*),
this is explained by conflating the meanings of "basis" (*āśraya*) and "support" (*niśraya*).
"Basis" refers to all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, which attain birth and abiding by depending upon causes and relying upon conditions.
All that which serves as a support or reliance is called an *āśraya* (basis),
such as when a king and his ministers rely upon one another.
If a phenomenon is determinate, possesses an object, and acts as a sovereign, it is [an *āśraya*].
That which causes the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects is the support;
namely, the six internal bases.
This is like a king and not like his ministers; therefore,
the simultaneous supports (sahabhū-āśraya) consist of only those [five],
while the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) has three supports.
This refers to the immediately preceding ceased mind;
all minds and mental factors rely upon this as their support,
for they necessarily do not arise apart from the guiding faculty.
There must be a conditioned dharma that acts as the primary factor to function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This [condition] opens up space for and guides the subsequent arising of mind and mental factors;
however, this [function] belongs solely to the mind and not to the mental factors and so forth.
If there were no possibility of this and that arising simultaneously,
one could say that this possesses the power of opening and guiding for that; however,
within a single body, the eight consciousnesses are already capable of arising together.
Therefore, only those of its own kind serve as the *āvedhaka-āśraya* (inducing support).
The Hīnayāna does not admit that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously;
rather, whenever any one of them arises, it is designated as "consciousness."
That which arises and ceases immediately is called the mind (manas).
Therefore, it is accepted that they serve as one another's equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
Consequently, the Mahāyāna school maintains that [the equal-and-immediate condition] consists only of its own kind.
Because there is necessarily no principle of simultaneous arising among those of the same category,
although mind and mental factors arise concurrently as distinct categories,
they correspond with and harmonize with one another such that they appear as a single unity.
The arising and ceasing of meditative concentration and its concomitant activities must necessarily be identical.
When one [moment] opens the way, the others also open the way;
yet, although they are able to open the way, they are not termed the "basis."
Because it does not maintain the doctrine of a self that is produced [by causes],
this differs in meaning from the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
First is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
It directly produces its own fruit as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
This entity has two aspects:
first, the seed (*bīja*).
Second is actualization.

As for "seeds," this refers to the functional distinctions within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) regarding the various realms, stages, and so forth, pertaining to the wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate [dharmas].
It is that which can induce a subsequent capacity of its own kind and produce a simultaneous manifest fruit of its own kind; this alone,
in relation to those [results], constitutes the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This refers to the meaning of the first of the three bases.
In relation to the manifest consciousness, it serves as the seed-base;
this includes the subsequent seeds as well, functioning as the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Manifesting entities refer to the seven evolving consciousnesses and their associated mental factors,
as well as the perceived objects and perceiving subjects, natures, elements, stages, and so forth, which they transform.
Excluding the wholesome states of the fruit of Buddhahood and the most inferior neutral states,
all others perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to produce seeds of their own kind;
this alone, in relation to those [seeds], constitutes the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
In all three bases, this principle does not apply:
manifesting states of the same category, when viewed in relation to one another, are never *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions),
because they arise from their own seeds.
Second is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*).

Because the preceding group [of moments] opens the way for its own subsequent class by arising without interval and so forth, causing them to arise with certainty, many seeds of the same kind function simultaneously.
It is known that those factors dissociated [from mind] are not included within this condition,
because they are extremely weak at the final moment when entry into cessation is complete and without remainder;
furthermore, there are no dharmas that arise subsequently as an equal-and-immediate condition.
Therefore, it is not this [ālayavijñāna] that serves as the condition;

rather, the other eight groups of consciousness— belonging to the three realms and nine stages, whether in the states of death and birth, or being with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava)—
mutually induce one another as appropriate to their respective conditions.
Therefore, all [of these] can function as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
which is precisely the meaning of the "opening-and-guiding support" (*āśraya*) among the three types of supports.
They also constitute the three types of object conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
That is to say, if there is a phenomenon that carries its own characteristic and is either the object of mental attention or the basis upon which the mind relies,
this entity is of two kinds.
First, the intimate; second, the remote.
If it is not separate in essence from the cognizing faculty, it is that which is internally relied upon as the object of consideration by the seeing-part and so forth.
It should be understood that this is the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Even though it is spatially separated from the substance of the cognizing subject,
it serves as the substantial basis (*ālambana*) for the internal object of cognition.
It should be understood that this is the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*).
The immediate object-condition (*sākṣātālambana-pratyaya*) exists in all cognitions,
because cognition necessarily does not arise apart from an internal basis upon which it relies.
Because the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) that is remote may exist even when the cognizing subject arises apart from an external object of consideration,
it follows that the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors [arise in this manner].
Each [of these consciousnesses] definitely possesses a direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*),
while the presence or absence of an indirect objective condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*) is indeterminate. This is because,
if it concerns the first five consciousnesses, they are coarse, dull, and weak.
Furthermore, because the seventh consciousness is innate (*sahaja*),
and because it must rely upon an external objective basis (*ālambana-pratyaya*) prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
it invariably possesses a remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
If the sixth consciousness has a sharp and intense mode of activity (ākāra),
it can operate with mastery in all states;
as for the bodies and lands transformed by the eighth consciousness:
They may be mutually enjoyed and serve as mutual collateral; however,
there is no principle for the transformed seeds of the sense faculties to be enjoyed by other sentient beings,
and thus they do not serve as mutual collateral.
Furthermore, in the stage where the five consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness have already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
the external substance upon which they rely may either exist or not exist;
thus, the presence or absence of the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) is indeterminate.
This explanation is given according to the essential nature of the various consciousnesses.
If one were to rely on their mutual presence or absence, the matter would be indeterminate;
fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have omitted such details.
Third, among the bases, none of these meanings exist.
Fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*):
this refers to any phenomenon that possesses superior power and efficacy.
Regarding other phenomena, whether they are concordant or discordant,
although the first three conditions are also sovereign (*adhipati*),
the fourth now excludes those and takes up the others.
In order to reveal that there are distinctions among various conditions,
these concordant and discordant characteristics operate across four locations,
because the four matters of arising, abiding, accomplishing, and attaining are distinct.
Although the predominant functions [of these faculties] are numerous according to their respective activities,
those that are most eminent and manifest are only twenty-two;
one should know that these are precisely the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
This subsumes the meaning of the "simultaneous support" (*sahabhū-āśraya*) among the three types of supports mentioned therein;
since this category is broad,
the eight consciousnesses serve as mutual conditions for one another.
Since the meanings of "possessing power" and "lacking power" apply to both cases,
regarding the meaning of "seed" within the first [type of] causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),
the seed is simply another name for habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Latent predispositions (vāsanā) necessarily exist by virtue of perfuming (bhāvanā).
On what basis is the term "perfuming" established?
Both the perfumer and the perfumed each possess four characteristics.
It is called "perfuming" (vāsanā) because it causes seeds to grow.
What are the four characteristics of that which is capable of perfuming?
First, it possesses arising and ceasing.
If a phenomenon is impermanent and is capable of performing the function of producing and growing latencies,
it is a perfuming agent;
this excludes unconditioned phenomena.
Because it is unchanging throughout its duration and lacks the function of growth or development, it is not a perfuming agent (*bhāvanā*).
Second, that which possesses superior efficacy:
if there is a power of arising and ceasing that is intense and capable of inducing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is a perfuming agent.
This refers to that which is capable of perfuming;
it excludes the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors,
because their power is too weak and inferior to serve as perfumers.
Third, there is increase and decrease.
That which possesses a superior function capable of increasing or decreasing and which encompasses the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) is the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*).
This excludes the fruit of Buddhahood;
because the perfected wholesome dharmas neither increase nor decrease, it is not a perfuming agent.
If that were a perfuming agent, it would not be perfected.
Consequently, there would have to be a distinction of superiority or inferiority between the preceding and succeeding states of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, [the transformation] proceeds in conjunction with that which is perfumed;
if it is simultaneous and co-spatial with that which is perfumed, it is neither identical to nor separate from it.
This refers to that which is capable of perfuming;
it excludes [the consciousness of] another person's body.
Because there is no sense of conjunction between preceding and succeeding moments, it is not capable of perfuming.
Only the seven evolving consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) possess the dominant power and function to undergo increase and decrease;
thus, being endowed with these four characteristics, they may serve as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).
What are the four characteristics of the perfumable object (*vāsayatva*)?
First, the nature of stable persistence:
if a phenomenon is of a uniform continuity from beginning to end and is capable of receiving habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
it is that which is perfumed.
This excludes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), sound, wind, and so forth;
because their nature is not stable and enduring, they are not perfumable (*abhāvya*).
Second, [they are excluded] because they are neutral (*avyākṛta*) by nature.
If a phenomenon is equal, without contradiction, and capable of accommodating habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
it is that which is perfumed;
this excludes both the wholesome and the defiled.
Because its power is so intense that it admits nothing else, it is not subject to perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Consequently, the Tathāgata’s eighth pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) carries only pre-existing seeds and does not receive new perfuming.
Third, the nature of being perfumable:
if a dharma is not of a sovereign nature, is not firm or dense, and is capable of receiving habitual tendencies (vāsanā),
it is that which is perfumable.
This excludes mental factors (*caitta*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because they are stable and dense, they are not susceptible to perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Fourth, [the seed] must possess the nature of being in conjunction with the perfuming agent (*bhāvaka*).
If it is simultaneous with and co-spatial to the perfuming agent, neither identical nor separate from it,
then it is a perfumable object;
this excludes [the perfumability of] other bodies.
Because there is no sense of conjunction between preceding and succeeding moments, [the mental factors] are not that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*).
Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), possessing these four characteristics, can be that which is perfumed;
it is not the case for the mental associates (*caitta*) and so forth.
If that is so, by what is the eighth consciousness perfumed?
Since the eighth is exclusively a consciousness that is perfumable (*bhāvyamāna*),
the answer is as follows:
That is to say, the aforementioned seven consciousnesses are produced through perfuming;
this is because it is taught that the seeds of their respective *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) are perfumed.
Specifically, the *nimitta-bhāga* arising from the first five consciousnesses is produced by depending upon the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, it perfumes the seeds of the object-aspect (nimittabhāga) of the eighth consciousness.
If the seventh consciousness arises by depending upon the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) of the eighth consciousness,
it therefore perfumes the seeds of the seeing-aspect of the eighth consciousness.
That sixth consciousness possesses both the objective and subjective aspects (nimitta-bhāga and darśana-bhāga) that condition the seeds of those very aspects within the eighth consciousness.
Since this conditioning has occurred continuously and without interruption since beginningless time,
there have consequently existed seeds of maturation (vipāka-bīja) from the very start of samsara.
If that is so, the eighth consciousness is not exclusively indeterminate,
because the seven perfuming consciousnesses pertain to all three natures.
Answer:
Because the fundamental substance upon which it relies is indeterminate (avyākṛta),
and because the manifested image-part (nimitta-bhāga) that arises from it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome,
the nature of the perfumed seeds (vāsanā-bīja) is exclusively indeterminate.
There are further questions and answers,
but fearing they would become too prolix, I have ceased them here.
Although their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are equal, the conditions upon which they rely are not the same.
Therefore, there is a distinction in the manner in which the eight consciousnesses are severed and their continuity maintained.
That is to say, the objects of the eight consciousnesses generally comprise ten types.
The first is the object of the common universal support (*āśraya*).
That is, it universally relies upon the faculties (*indriya*),
because those manifesting consciousnesses rely upon the seed-consciousness.
Second, it is the basis and object-condition for defilement and purification.
This refers to the faculties of defilement and purity;
because they function in dependence upon objects of defilement and purity,
they constitute the basis and the object for the three kinds of discrimination.
That is, they are distinguished by their faculties (*indriya*),
because the discriminating mind takes form and so forth as its objects.
Fourth, the uncommon basis and object.
These are the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Since consciousness must arise only when the faculty and its object coexist,
these five primarily function as the conditions for their own respective cognitions.
This refers precisely to the seed,
because the substance of consciousness must arise directly from the seed.
The sixth [condition] is the stirring that causes it to arise as an object-condition.
This refers precisely to attention (*manasikāra*),
because it has the capacity to alert the mind that is being induced.
Seventh is the objective condition of attraction (*ākṣepa-pratyaya*).
This refers to the objective referent (*ālambana*).
Because consciousness arises only when drawn by an object,
it is called the "opening and guiding condition" that causes [consciousness] to arise.
This means that because the preceding moment of consciousness, as it is about to cease, can induce the arising of the subsequent moment.
Ninth, the non-obstructive condition for arising,
which refers to space itself.
If there were obstructions, one would be unable to discern; thus,
the tenth is illumination that causes the perception of conditions,
which is to say, light itself.
Because one cannot see in the dark,
visual consciousness herein possesses ten conditions;
if any one of them is lacking, it will certainly not arise.
The auditory faculty possesses nine conditions;
that is to say, with the exception of light,
because one is able to hear even in darkness.
The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body each possess eight conditions;
in all cases, space is excluded because they perceive their objects through contact.
The sixth consciousness possesses only six conditions;
it excludes the five material sense-faculties,
as it does not rely upon them.
This is because, apart from the faculty of discrimination,
it is its very own substance.
If the eighth consciousness possesses five conditions:
Excluding the sixth consciousness and those [consciousnesses] that depend on the universal sense-faculties,
the eighth does not depend on an intermittent consciousness,
nor can its own substance depend upon itself.
If the seventh consciousness possesses only four conditions,
the object-condition is excluded,
because its object is none other than its own supporting faculty and lacks a separate substance.
It is said that because [the mind] functions in dependence upon them and takes them as its objects,
there are differences in the severance of permanence and existence based on the greater or fewer number of conditions relied upon.
Consequently, the universality or restriction of the three realms also differs.
That is to say, the first five consciousnesses have coarse and active modes of activity;
they are incapable of reflection and function solely toward external objects,
arising in dependence upon many conditions.
Because the various conditions upon which they depend are frequently incomplete,
their arising is brief while their interruption is frequent. Thus,
the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses belong exclusively to the Desire Realm.
Because there is no visible form, odor, or taste, and because there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*),
the three consciousnesses— eye, ear, and nose— do not function in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Those who have become weary of form are born in those heavens.
Because it lacks both form-faculties and form-objects,
although there is form that is the fruit of meditative concentration, there is no form that is the fruit of karma.
Even when one reaches the state of Buddhahood, the pure consciousness associated with the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done) is still subject to interruption.
Because its conventional objects of perception are subject to cessation,
although the sixth consciousness is likewise coarse and active,
it is capable of independent reflection and operates through both internal and external gates without depending on numerous conditions.
Furthermore, since the requisite conditions are never absent,
it should be able to manifest at all times;
it also pervades the practices of all stages throughout the three realms.
Due to adverse conditions,
they are severed and extinguished at five stages;
therefore, they arise frequently, while they do not arise infrequently.

What are the five states? They are: birth in the Heaven of Non-conception—which is the aforementioned maturation of the signless—as well as the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception.
Regarding sleep, fainting,
and so forth, the definitions of these five states are as explained below.
As for the pure consciousness associated with the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of profound observation) upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, it is eternally uninterrupted.
Because it contemplates both the ultimate and the conventional at all times,
if the seventh consciousness has been a single, continuous stream from beginningless time, constantly uninterrupted,
it also pervades all stages within the three realms.
Because it serves as the basis for the ālayavijñāna and other consciousnesses,
yet it undergoes transformation during three states:
namely, those of the arhat and the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Within the supramundane path, there is no distinction between defiled and pure portions;
the manas is likewise uninterrupted,
and the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) arises in constant association.
Because it constantly takes as its object the principle of the equality of the ultimate and conventional truths,
if the eighth consciousness is in the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*),
it perpetually evolves like a flowing stream throughout the nine stages of the three realms.
The term "constant" (nitya) excludes cessation;
conversely, it expresses non-constancy.
It is just like a violent torrent, for such is the natural law (dharmatā) of cause and effect.
Neither annihilated nor eternal, this is the principle of dependent origination; therefore,
it serves as the retributive substance for rebirth in the realms of existence,
pervading all stages within the three worlds.
Due to the differences in designation across the three stages— contaminated, uncontaminated, and beyond training—
the entity [of the ālayavijñāna] is either relinquished or not relinquished according to those designations.

Specifically, at the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) in the two vehicles, and at the seventh ground of the bodhisattva, the name "ālayavijñāna" is relinquished, while the entity of the "ripening consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*) is not.
The Bodhisattva relinquishes it when about to attain enlightenment;
the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha relinquish it upon entering the nirvana without remainder;
however, the essence of the immaculate consciousness (amala-vijñāna) has no time of relinquishment.
Because it is constantly associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;
because the reflections of all wholesome dharmas are perpetually present before it;
and because its benefit and joy for sentient beings have no end.
However, the meanings and distinctions of the eight consciousnesses are boundless;
fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I shall briefly indicate the essential framework.
Treatise:
Second, the mental factors (caitta) are briefly of fifty-one kinds. The commentary states:
Next, secondly, the mental factors are explained.
This section contains three parts.
First, the total number is presented collectively;
second, they are categorized into six stages;
finally, they are enumerated individually according to each stage.
This is the first [section].
However, regarding the opening and closing of these mental factors (*caitta*) across various treatises:
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are fifty-three.
Furthermore, regarding wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*):
just as wrong mindfulness (*mithyā-smṛti*) and wrong wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*) are included among the afflictions (*kleśa*),
the same principle applies to wrong desire and wrong resolve.
If one follows the *Pañcaskandhaka-prakaraṇa*, there are fifty-five [mental factors];
therein, "wrong desire" (*mithyā-chanda*) and so forth are combined and included within the "object-specific" (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*) category,
while "wrong view" (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) is divided into five types.
Although both are wisdom (*prajñā*),
because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ,
this [wisdom] and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) [are distinct].
Both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācāśāstra* state that there are fifty-one [mental factors] based on the sense of their being combined;
this is because the five views are all unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*),
and although their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ, they do not have distinct entities.
They are subsumed under right mindfulness and wisdom along with the five wholesome roots.
Since wrong mindfulness and wisdom act as obstacles to them,
and because their faults are grave, they are categorized separately as afflictions.
The wholesome desire and so forth do not enter among the roots of goodness;
because their obstructions are slight, they are included among the object-specific [mental factors].
According to the sūtras relied upon by the Hīnayāna, there are forty-six [factors].
Furthermore, the meaning of the synthesis will be explained below as it appears in the treatise. The treatise states:
"There are five universal [mental factors], five object-specific ones, eleven wholesome ones, six afflictions, twenty secondary afflictions, and four indeterminate ones. Kai says:
These are the six categories of mental states.
They are so designated because they can certainly be found within all minds,
and because they arise by taking various distinct objects as their conditions.
Because it can only arise within a wholesome state of mind;
because its nature is subsumed under the root afflictions;
and because it is exclusively of the nature of an outflow from the afflictions.
Because they are indeterminate with respect to being wholesome, defiled,
and so forth, there are thus six distinct stages.
If the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* combines them collectively, there are five.
Since both primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*),
the five distinctions are established by means of four types of "all" (*sarva*):
namely, all in terms of nature (*svabhāva*), all in terms of time (*kāla*), and all in terms of coexistence (*sahabhū*).
Among the five categories, the universal mental factors possess all four types of "all-inclusiveness" (sarvatraga).
The object-specific factors possess only the first two types.
The wholesome factors possess only one.
That is to say, in all stages,
four types of defilement are entirely absent;
only one type of indeterminate [defilement] exists.
This refers to all natures,
distinguished by these five categories; furthermore,
there are these six categories of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Although various treatises clarify this matter, none do so completely.
Since the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) provides the most perfect and lucid explanation,
the following text will rely strictly upon that commentary.
Treatise:
The five universal [mental factors] are: first, attention; second, contact; third, sensation; fourth, perception; and fifth, volition. The Commentary says:
The following section lists them individually according to their respective stages.
Within this, the six stages are divided into six [factors].
This is the first [category], the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
*Manasikāra* (attention) has the nature of being able to alert the mind.
Its function is to direct the mind toward its focal object.
That is to say, it alerts the seeds of the mind that are to arise and directs them toward the object;
therefore, it is called *manasikāra* (attention).
Although this [karma] can also induce mental factors (*caitta*),
because the mind (*citta*) is primary, it is said only to induce the mind.
"Action" (*karman*) means striking or impelling.
"Manas" (the mind) refers to the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*);
it is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound) because it acts as the agent.
"Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the discrimination of the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three.
It has the nature of causing the mind and mental factors to contact their objects,
and its function is to serve as the basis for sensation, perception, volition, and so forth. That is to say,
because the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness mutually accord with one another, it is called the "threefold conjunction" (trikasamnipāta).
Because contact arises based on them and causes them to harmonize, it is said to belong to them.
At the stage of the threefold conjunction, the capacity to give rise to mental factors is present; this is termed "transformation."
Contact (sparśa) is called "discrimination" because it arises from those [three conditions];
its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is that which brings all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) into conjunction with their respective objects.
Since it appears to function as a mental factor that arises in accordance [with its object],
its activity consists in serving as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors].
Feeling has the nature of experiencing the characteristics of objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral.
Its function is to give rise to craving,
for it can produce the desire for union, separation, or neither.
Perception (saṃjñā) has the nature of grasping the image of an object.
Its function is the establishment of various conventional designations (*nāma-paññatti*);
that is to say, one must first establish the specific characteristics and limits of an object before being able to subsequently give rise to various conventional designations.
Volition (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in purposeful activity.
It takes the mind as its object and functions as its activity; that is,
it can apprehend the objective sphere and the characteristics of correct causes and so forth,
driving and directing one's own mind to perform wholesome actions and the like.
When the mindless [states] arise, these five do not coexist;
therefore, these five are called "universal" (sarvatraga),
because they function universally throughout all states of mind.
In the treatises of the Hīnayāna, these are termed the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

As for the five object-specific factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata*), they are: first, desire (*chanda*); second, resolve (*adhimokṣa*); third, mindfulness (*smṛti*); fourth, concentration (*samādhi*); and fifth, wisdom (*prajñā*). Kai says:
This enumerates the specific object-conditions (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*).
Because the objects they perceive are for the most part different,
they are discussed next among the six categories.
What is called "desire" (chanda) has the nature of longing for an object of pleasure,
and its function is to serve as the basis for diligence (vīrya).
The "object of desire" refers to an object that one wishes to contemplate.
Regarding all things, when there is a wish to investigate them,
desire arises only because there is an aspiration for them.
If one does not wish to observe [an object] but instead engages with it spontaneously according to the power of its causes,
there is a total absence of desire;
for this reason, it is said that desire is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).
If the desire for wholesome dharmas can arouse right effort,
because that [desire] assists in accomplishing all wholesome matters,
the treatise states that the function of this effort is to serve as a basis.
As for "resolute confidence" (adhimokṣa),
its nature is the confirmation and maintenance of a determined object;
its function is to be unshakeable by others.
Through the power of reasoning and scriptural authority regarding what is erroneous or correct, one definitively ascertains and maintains the apprehended object;
because it cannot be diverted by other conditions,
there is a complete absence of doubt regarding that object.
It is neither a resolved determination nor a resolute conviction;
therefore, this resolute conviction is also not omnipresent.
As for what is called "mindfulness":
Its nature is to cause the mind to clearly remember and not forget objects previously experienced;
its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That is to say, it repeatedly recollects and maintains objects that have been previously perceived.
Because it prevents the loss of that which induces meditative concentration,
one does not give rise to any recollection regarding objects of a type never before experienced;
even regarding those previously experienced, one is unable to remember them clearly.
Mindfulness also does not arise [in that state].
Therefore, mindfulness is certainly not subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
As for meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
This is called samādhi; that is, it is concentration which evenly holds the mind upon the object of observation,
having as its nature the focused attention of the mind without distraction.
Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*).
That is to say, by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it causes the mind to focus one-pointedly without distraction upon an object that consists of qualities, faults, or neither;
based on this, there arises the wisdom of discernment (*viniścaya-jñāna*).
If the mind is not focused intently upon its object, concentration does not arise; therefore, it is not a universal mental factor.
As for what is called "wisdom":
Its nature is the discernment of the object under investigation,
and its function is the severing of doubt;
that is to say, because one attains certainty through the investigative pursuit of wisdom regarding objects that possess qualities, defects, or neither.
Because they lack discernment within a mind that is ignorant regarding objects that are not the domain of contemplation, they are not included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Nevertheless, the treatises of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) likewise designate them as "universal" and include them among the "great ground" (*mahābhūmika*) factors.
Because those whose minds are pervaded by these [views] have not yet realized the principle,
they are refuted as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
However, these five types may arise either individually or collectively.
This means that based on what is desired, one gives rise only to desire;
up to and including, based on what is observed, one gives rise only to concentration and wisdom;
or they arise together as appropriate, mutually supporting one another.
This refers to the state where, regarding a desired, determined, and previously familiar object of observation,
two, three, four, or five among desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom arise;
or there may be mental states in which none of these five arise at all.
Just as when the mind suddenly encounters objects that are neither of the four [neutral] types, both [the mind and its associated states] are associated with the five feelings;
for one desires to escape from matters of suffering and sorrow,
and one desires to unite with matters of joy and pleasure.
Because there is also the aspiration for equality toward these matters.
The other meanings associated with this should be explained accordingly.
Furthermore, these five are based on nature (*dhātu*), realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), and so forth.
The meanings of the other categories should be reflected upon according to reason.

The treatise states: "The eleven wholesome [factors] are: first, faith; second, shame; third, remorse; fourth, non-greed; fifth, non-hatred; sixth, non-delusion; seventh, diligence; eighth, pliancy; ninth, heedfulness; tenth, equanimity; and eleventh, non-harming. Kai says:
This reveals that there are eleven mental factors in the wholesome state;
those that coexist exclusively with a wholesome mind are termed "wholesome mental factors.
Therefore, faith, shame, and so forth definitely number eleven.
What is called faith has the nature of deep acceptance,
aspiration, and desire for reality, virtue, and capability, with mental purity as its essence;
its function is to counteract lack of faith and to delight in the wholesome.
However, the distinctions of faith are briefly of three kinds.
First is faith in existence and reality,
which refers to the profound faith and acceptance regarding the actual entities and principles of all phenomena.
Second, faith in possessing virtue,
which means having deep faith and delight in the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels.
Third, faith in possessing capability.
This refers to having deep faith that all mundane and supramundane virtues have the power to be attained and accomplished, thereby giving rise to aspiration. By means of this,
it counteracts lack of faith (*āśraddhya*),
so that the mind comes to delight in realizing and practicing mundane and supramundane virtues.
"Patience" (kṣānti) refers to resolute conviction (adhimukti), which is the cause of faith;
"delightful desire" (chanda) refers to aspiration (icchā), which is the fruit of faith.
This nature is lucid and is able to purify the mind and its associated factors.
Because the mind is predominant, it is designated by the name "purity of mind.
Just as the water-purifying jewel can clarify turbid water,
although shame and the other [wholesome roots] are virtuous, they do not have purity as their defining characteristic.
This purity serves as its defining characteristic to avoid the fault of confusion with other states.
Furthermore, while each defiled dharma has its own distinct characteristic,
it is only lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) whose intrinsic nature is turbidity.
Furthermore, it can turbidify other minds and mental factors,
just as an extremely filthy object defiles both itself and others.
Since faith is the direct opposite of that, its characteristic is purity.
That which is called *hrī* (moral shame) has the nature of revering and honoring the noble and the good by relying on the power of oneself and the Dharma;
its function is to counteract lack of shame and to bring rest to unwholesome conduct.
This refers to relying on the excellence and supremacy of one's own dharma;
it is the honoring of the virtuous and good, and the feeling of shame regarding faults and evils.
It serves as the antidote to lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and brings all unwholesome conduct to rest.
What is called *hrī* (moral shame) has as its nature the rejection of violence and evil through the power of worldly standards;
its function is to counteract *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread) and to bring about the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
This refers to relying on the predominance of worldly censure and revulsion to reject and repel violence and evil,
and through shame regarding transgressions and offenses,
to counteract non-embarrassment and bring rest to unwholesome conduct.
Shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) share the common characteristic of being a sense of shame regarding faults and evils; for both involve feeling ashamed.
Their distinct characteristics consist in the former’s quality of reverence and esteem, and the latter’s quality of rejection and aversion.
Because shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) arise separately,
whenever a wholesome mind arises, it possesses the sense of honoring what is good and rejecting what is evil regardless of the object encountered. Therefore,
both shame and dread of blame are universal to all wholesome minds.
Non-attachment is defined as having the nature of non-clinging toward existence and the requisites for existence;
its function is to counteract attachment and to act as a basis for the performance of wholesome deeds.
Regarding "non-hatred":
its intrinsic nature is the absence of malice toward suffering and the instruments of suffering;
its function is to counteract hatred and to perform wholesome deeds.
When a wholesome mind arises,
regardless of whatever object it encounters, it remains without attachment or aversion toward existence and so forth; thus,
the establishment of [the perception of] existence and so forth does not necessarily require taking that [object] as its focal point.
As previously established through the contemplation of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) regarding good and evil,
these two factors both pervade all wholesome states of mind.
Regarding the term "non-delusion" (*amoha*):
Its nature is the clear understanding of all principles and phenomena;
its function is to counteract ignorance and to perform wholesome deeds.
Some say that wisdom has the nature of the absence of ignorance.
Because wisdom exists even when one does not encounter delusion,
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* does not establish non-delusion as a separate factor;
it is because non-delusion is subsumed within the universal mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, only ten types are taught as the universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*).
Some say that non-delusion (*amoha*) has a distinct intrinsic nature and does not have wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.
It directly opposes ignorance,
just as non-attachment and non-hatred are subsumed under the roots of goodness.
As for what is called diligence:
Its nature is valor in the practice of cultivation and abandonment regarding wholesome and unwholesome categories.
Its function is to counteract laziness and fulfill the wholesome.
"Valor" indicates spiritual progress and distinguishes it from all defiled phenomena.
"Resolute, manifesting as pure, simple,
and neutral" indicates that diligence is comprised exclusively within the nature of the wholesome.
There are briefly five types of distinctions regarding its characteristics.
What is called the preparatory practice of donning the armor is characterized by being without inferiority, without regression, and without satiety;
this is due to the distinctions of its initial arousal of the mind, its long duration, its uninterrupted continuity, its earnestness, and its cultivation without remainder.
Regarding pliancy (*praśrabdhi*):
its nature is to be free from heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*), bringing the body and mind into a state of harmony and adaptability.
Its function is to counteract lethargy (*styāna*) and to effect the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*).
This means that it subdues and eliminates those factors that obstruct meditative concentration,
thereby causing the basis [of consciousness] to become transformed into a state of ease;
therefore, this pliancy exists only within the stages of meditative concentration.
Because the state of being "harmonious and expansive" regarding body and mind does not exist in other stages,
this [first] wholesome mind alone is not universal;
apart from this, the remaining ten wholesome minds arise universally.
Non-negligence (*apramāda*) has the nature of guarding and cultivating that which is to be abandoned and cultivated through the three roots of diligence.
It serves as the antidote to negligence and brings to fulfillment all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.
That is to say, it is precisely these four factors that are capable of guarding against and cultivating the tasks of abandonment and cultivation; this is termed "heedfulness" (apramāda).
It does not possess a separate substantial entity, as there is no distinct characteristic.
Since there is no distinct function apart from the four capacities regarding the prevention of unwholesome deeds and the cultivation of wholesome ones,
it is called "equanimity."
The three roots of diligence have the nature of causing the mind to abide in equanimity, rectitude, and effortlessness.
Their function is to counteract restlessness and to establish the mind in tranquility.
The distinctions among the stages of equanimity, rectitude, and effortlessness are explained according to their initial, middle, and final phases.
Through heedfulness (*apramāda*), one first eliminates the various defilements;
subsequently, through equanimity (*upekṣā*), one causes the mind to abide in tranquility.
This [equanimity] has no separate substantial entity, just like heedfulness.
Because apart from those four dharmas there is no functioning of signlessness;
because that which can cause tranquility is precisely those four dharmas;
and because that which is caused to become tranquil is precisely the mind and so forth.
Regarding non-harming (*avihiṃsā*):
it has the nature of not causing injury or affliction to sentient beings and being free from hatred;
its function is to counteract harming and to manifest compassion.
This refers to non-hatred itself;
not causing harm or affliction toward sentient beings is conventionally designated as "non-violence" (avihiṃsā).
Non-hatred is the direct opposite of the hatred that leads to the taking of life.
Non-harming (ahiṃsā) is the direct opposite of harming sentient beings through injury or affliction;
non-anger (avyāpāda) consists in bestowing happiness,
while non-harming consists in uprooting suffering.
This is called the distinction between these two coarse characteristics.
In reality, non-hatred possesses a truly existent intrinsic nature;
non-violence is a provisional designation based on a portion of that [non-hatred].
In order to clarify the distinct characteristics of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
and because they are superior in bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings,
non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is established separately, with both its conventional and ultimate natures explained.
Therefore, among the eleven wholesome [factors], the last three are provisional,
while the first eight are substantially existent,
because their characteristics and functions are distinct.
If that were so, then delight, aversion, non-conceit, non-doubt, non-pride, non-deception, and so forth, would not be wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*).
Answer:
Although they are all subsumed within the wholesome, they possess no separate substantial entities (*dravya*).
If their characteristics and functions differ, they are established separately;
other wholesome factors are not like this,
and thus should not be taken as an analogy.
Furthermore, among the various defiled dharmas, those that pervade all six consciousnesses are predominant;
therefore, in contrast to them, wholesome dharmas are established as distinct categories.
Pride, anger, and so forth, however, are associated exclusively with the mental consciousness.
Although harmfulness is likewise [a fault], it is established as non-harming (avihiṃsā) by way of its contrary because it frequently arises and causes affliction to others,
and because it obstructs compassion, the superior cause for the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
thus, its predominant defects are understood in order to eliminate them.
Lapse of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*),
and lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*) are not mentioned among the distinct mental factors (*viśeṣaviṣaya*) of the wholesome category.
Since the pure and the defiled are opposites, how could the pure factors be fewer than the defiled?
Because the pure is superior while the defiled is inferior, and because the adversary is few while [the objects] are many.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that,
according to principle, it is permissible to speak of "many" as being of the same substance.
The categories of mental factors (*caitasika*) are numerous according to their specific characteristics;
therefore, one should not demand uniformity regarding their association with either defiled or pure states.
The tenth [mental factor] is associated with all five types of feeling (*vedanā*).
First, it eliminates sorrow and suffering,
namely through pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
for there is the experience of oppression due to a lack of composure and ease.
This [mental factor] can be associated with all the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*),
because it is not incompatible with faith (*śraddhā*) and the like, nor with desire (*chanda*) and the like; however,
it is not associated with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
The remaining [faculties] pertain to all three realms;
they are all of the three types—learner, non-learner, and neither—and are not abandoned by insight.
This is because it is taught that they are abandoned only through cultivation and are not abandoned [by insight].
The analysis of the remaining categories should be considered according to reason as appropriate.
The treatise states:
"The six root afflictions are: first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, doubt; and sixth, wrong view. The commentary says:
This reveals the six types of fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
Because these six types are particularly heavy by nature,
they disturb and distress the body and mind of sentient beings.
Because they are able to give rise to the various secondary afflictions such as anger and so forth,
they are called "root afflictions" (*mūlakleśa*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* refers to them as the "great affliction ground dharmas" (*mahākleśabhūmikadharma*).
Only delusion (*moha*) alone is the same as in this treatise;

the other five— namely, negligence (*pramāda*), laziness (*kausīdya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)— are included among these great secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-kleśa*).
Because they universally defile the mind and cause it to be troubled and tormented by feverish distress,
they are called the "great afflictive dharmas.
They are subsumed within greed, hatred, pride, doubt, and the indeterminate factors.
Because wrong views are not established as distinct from wisdom,
this is a point of difference between the tenets of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools.
As for what is called "greed":
Its nature is attachment to existence and the instruments of existence;
its function is to obstruct non-attachment and to give rise to suffering,
because the aggregates of grasping arise through the power of craving.
That which is called "hatred" has as its nature a stained aversion and resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering;
its function is to obstruct non-hatred and to serve as the basis for unease and unwholesome conduct.
This means that hatred necessarily causes heat and affliction to body and mind,
because it gives rise to various evil karmas of an unwholesome nature.
As for what is called delusion:
Regarding all principles and phenomena, its nature is described as darkness (*tamas*).
Its function is to obstruct non-delusion and to serve as the basis for all defilements.
This means that through ignorance (*avidyā*), doubt, false resolve, craving, and other primary and secondary afflictions arise, which are capable of summoning the defiled dharmas of future rebirths.
What is called pride (*māna*) has the nature of being haughty toward others by relying on oneself;
its function is to obstruct non-pride and to produce suffering.
This refers to the state where one who possesses pride does not humble their mind before virtues or those endowed with virtue;
because of this, they revolve endlessly in the cycle of birth and death and undergo all manner of suffering.
This pride is differentiated into seven or nine types.
That is to say, it arises with respect to the three categories of self,
qualities, and objects.
What is called "doubt" has the nature of indecision regarding the principles of the truths.
Its function is to obstruct the absence of doubt regarding wholesome qualities.
That is to say, because of doubt, wisdom fails to reach a decision;
since the mind harbors hesitation, wholesome states do not arise.
Wrong view has as its nature defiled wisdom that erroneously speculates upon the principles of the truths;
its function is to obstruct right vision and to bring about suffering.
This means that those with wrong views undergo much suffering.
There are five distinct types of this view's mode of activity:
first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
It refers to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for all speculative views.
There are twenty types and sixty-five such distinctions of these views.
It is subsumed under that which arises from discrimination:
the view of extremes.
This refers to the adherence to either annihilationism or eternalism with respect to those very [objects], and its function is to obstruct the middle way and the path of deliverance.
This is the distinction among views.
Among the various types of views,
there are those that adhere to the four theories of universal permanence regarding the past.
There are four theories that one part is eternal;
sixteen theories regarding the existence of perception in the future limit;
and eight theories each concerning non-perception and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The seven [types of] annihilationism and so forth are subsumed under conceptual arising;
they consist of three types of wrong view.
This refers to the denial of cause, effect, activity, and substantial entities,
as well as all other false attachments apart from the four views;
this is because the designation and meaning of "dominant condition" (adhipati-pratyaya) are all-encompassing.
This is the distinction among views.
Among the various types of views,
there are those that cling to the past and maintain two theories of causelessness.
The four types of pride and delusion regarding immortality, such as the view of finitude;
the five views concerning the future limit that reckon in nirvana in the present life;
or the reckoning of Īśvara, Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, and other such entities as being eternal and unchanging.
Some reckon that Īśvara and others are the cause of all things;
some recklessly speculate on various false liberations;
and some falsely cling to what is not the path as being the path.
All other such views as these are subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Fourth is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),
which refers to [the attachment] toward all views and the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which they depend.
It functions by grasping [wrong views] as supreme and capable of bringing about purification, and it serves as the basis for all forms of contention. This is the fifth:
the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
It refers to the grasping at views, ascetic rules and observances,
and their underlying aggregates as being supreme and capable of bringing about purification;
its function is to serve as the basis for fruitless exertion and suffering.
Among these ten afflictions, both general and specific,
greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), as well as doubt (*vicikitsā*), certainly do not arise simultaneously;
for the objects of affection and aversion must necessarily be different.
Because it is indeterminate regarding its object and lacks defiled attachment,
it may be associated with pride and the five views;
for the objects that are defiled by or relied upon by it are functional.
Because all objects of the five views are desirable,
hatred (*dveṣa*) and pride (*māna*), or doubt (*vicikitsā*), may arise together with them;
for the objects that are despised or loathed can be the same as those [of the views].
Because one becomes enraged when long contemplating [the object] without reaching a decision,
these two views are necessarily not associated with the latter two [views]. This is because,
while grasping [the path] as the supreme way, one does not feel hatred toward it.
It may be associated with the first three views;
for by grasping at the aggregates of suffering and pleasure as being either self or annihilated, one gives rise to aversion and anger.
Wrong view, moreover, denies and slanders the existence of good and evil phenomena.
Because hatred may exist while one is in a state of meditative concentration,
whereas doubt does not,
there is no sense of association between pride and doubt.
However, it can be associated with all five views,
because their modes of activity (ākāra) do not contradict one another.
Doubt (vicikitsā), being characterized by a lack of definitive resolution, contradicts the nature of views.
Doubt and views certainly do not arise together;
the five views are necessarily not associated with one another,
because there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom within a single moment of consciousness.
Delusion is associated with all nine types [of mental factors],
because the arising of all afflictions necessarily depends upon delusion,
and because there is a distinction between those that are co-emergent and those that are conceptual.
Because their natures, fetters, realms, stages, and so forth differ in terms of being universal or specific,
among these ten afflictions— both general and particular—
six are both innate and arise partially.
Because they can all arise through spontaneous reflection,
the three views following doubt arise solely from conceptual discrimination;
they require the influence of evil friends and false teachings.
Because they arise only through self-examination and reflection,
these two afflictions pertain to all three realms and accordingly possess both the natures of unwholesome and neutral.
If it is associated with the desire realm and arises from conceptual discrimination,
it is subsumed solely under the unwholesome,
because it gives rise to evil conduct.
If these verses give rise to unwholesome karma,
they are likewise not well-restrained,
for they harm both oneself and others.
The remainder are comprised within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because they are subtle, do not obstruct the wholesome, and do not excessively harm oneself or others.
As for those in the two higher realms, they are comprised exclusively within the indeterminate.
Because that which is suppressed by the power of meditative concentration does not give rise to evil;
from this it is known that anger exists only in the desire realm.
This is because its nature is unwholesome, as it harms both oneself and others.
The others pertain to all three realms because they pertain to both natures;
they arise in a lower stage while one has not yet abandoned the defilements of that lower stage.
The afflictions of the higher stages do not manifest;
only one who has attained the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of that stage is able to suppress the various delusions of the lower stages so that they do not arise.
Because the afflictions of the higher stages may manifest there,
all afflictions of the lower stages— both those arising from discrimination and those that are innate— are capable of manifesting when one is born in a higher stage.
One who is born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna falls into hell because they have slandered liberation; thus,
while their body is still in the higher realm, they are about to descend to be reborn there.
Because the innate craving that arises to moisten rebirth in a lower realm exists,
the afflictions of a lower stage also take a higher stage as their object;
for one craves the flavor of the higher meditative absorptions of those upper stages.

Since it has already been stated that hatred, resentment, and envy take the Path and Cessation as their objects, one should also acknowledge that they take the stage of detachment from desire (*vairāgyabhūmi*) as their object.

Furthermore, those who grasp at a self or what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya*), or who hold views of annihilationism, eternalism, or pride, take all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their general object; because these [defilements] can take the higher stages as their objects.
The principle that the remaining five [afflictions] take the higher [realms] as their objects is fully established.
Furthermore, the afflictions of the higher realms also take the lower realms as their objects;
for it is said that those born in a higher realm look down upon sentient beings in the lower realms, relying on their own superior qualities to disparage them.

Because those who grasp at self and what belongs to self by taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as their object, and who cling to [the extremes of] annihilation or permanence, take lower objects as their basis;
this should be understood accordingly for doubt and the latter three views.
If one were to analyze them, they are abandoned only through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
Because that which is coarse is easy to sever;
if it were innate, it would be severed only through cultivation,
because that which is subtle is difficult to sever.
Therefore, the afflictions associated with the manas-consciousness are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
because they are extremely subtle;
yet they are not non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).
Because they are defiled,
the ten [afflictions] abandoned by insight are actually severed simultaneously;
although there are general and specific, direct and indirect ways of being deluded regarding the truths.
Since the true path of seeing takes the truths as its collective object,
there are both collective and individual aspects to the manner in which it is deluded regarding those truths;
"collective" refers to ten types.
They are all deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths;
for suffering and its origin are the basis and cause of that [delusion],
while cessation and the path are the objects of their fear.
The distinction is as follows: two [of these views] arise from delusion regarding the characteristics of the Four Truths, while eight arise from delusion regarding all four.

The view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) arise only with respect to the fruit; this is because the specific aspects of emptiness and non-self belong to the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the truths that are objects of delusion, there are those that are proximate and those that are remote.
Specifically, doubt and three of the views are proximately deluded regarding the principle of suffering.

The two graspings—clinging to views and clinging to precepts and observances—grasp those three views, as well as the precepts and observances and the aggregates upon which they depend, as being supreme and capable of purification.
Regarding the views of self and others, as well as their associated retinues, greed, hatred,
and pride arise respectively according to the circumstances; these,
together with the non-afflictive ignorance associated with them, constitute the ninefold delusion.
Non-associated ignorance is directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering;
doubt and false view are directly deluded regarding the truth of origination and so forth;
and the two types of grasping, craving, and the rest should be understood accordingly based on [the analysis of] suffering.
However, hatred (*dveṣa*) can also directly delude one regarding cessation and the path,
because one gives rise to aversion and jealousy out of fear of them.
Such are the coarse characteristics of the direct and indirect ways in which the [afflictions] delude one regarding the Truths.
The detailed categorization is as clarified in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is both sudden and gradual abandonment,
depending on whether the faculties of the three vehicles are sharp or dull.
Regarding the afflictions associated with the sixth consciousness:
for one class of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, each of the nine grades within each of the nine stages of the three realms is severed gradually and individually;
for another class of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, the nine grades of the nine stages of the three realms are combined into a single aggregate and severed individually.
If the afflictions associated with the manas-consciousness are abandoned all at once together with the lowest-of-the-low afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
it is because they are the most subtle.

A Bodhisattva must reach the vajropama-samādhi (diamond-like concentration), wherein, in a single moment, the afflictions of the seventh consciousness (manas) pertaining to all nine stages of the three realms are severed simultaneously and instantaneously.
Such is the essential meaning of these ten afflictions.
The meanings of the other categories are explained extensively in the treatise.
Regarding the statement in the treatise that there are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):

1. Anger, 2. Resentment, 3. Malice, 4. Concealment, 5. Deceit, 6. Guile, 7. Arrogance, 8. Harmfulness, 9. Envy, 10. Avarice, 11. Lack of shame, 12. Lack of dread, 13. Lack of faith, 14. Laziness, 15. Heedlessness, 16. Torpor, 17. Agitation, 18. Loss of mindfulness, 19. Lack of clear comprehension, 20. Distraction. Kai said:
This concludes the fifth category of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
These twenty types are called secondary afflictions because they are merely specific states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the primary afflictions and are of the nature of their outflow (*niṣyanda*).
However, these twenty categories are divided into three types.
Specifically, because the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*) arise individually, they are called the "minor secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*).
In the *Abhidharmakośa*, these are termed the "mental factors of the stage of minor secondary afflictions" (*upakleśabhūmikadharma*).
The two [mental factors] beginning with lack of shame (āhrīkya) are called "intermediate secondary afflictions" because they pervade all unwholesome states;
in the *Abhidharmakośa*, these are termed the "great unwholesome mental factors" (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*).
The eight [factors] beginning with lack of faith (āśraddhya) are called "great secondary afflictions" because they pervade all defiled minds.
The *Abhidharmakośa* does not include these among the great secondary afflictions (*mahā-āveṇika-kleśa*),
because the first five are subsumed under the great afflictions (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*),
and the latter three lack a distinct substantial entity.
What is called anger (*krodha*) has the nature of being an outburst of indignation toward a presently manifest object that is harmful;
its function is to obstruct freedom from anger and to lead to the grasping of weapons.
This is because those who harbor resentment frequently manifest violent and evil bodily *vijñapti*-karma.
As for what is called "enmity" (*upanāha*),
its nature consists of harboring malice without relinquishing it, forming a grudge preceded by anger.
Its function is to obstruct the absence of resentment and to produce feverish affliction (*paridāha*).
This is because one who harbors a grudge is unable to exercise forbearance and is constantly tormented by heat.
As for what is called "affliction" (*upāyāsa*):
Preceded by anger and resentment, it has the nature of being pursued by contact, intense heat, and stubborn perversity;
its function is to obstruct non-annoyance and [to act like] stinging insects.

That is to say, because one pursues past evils and encounters present adverse conditions, the mind becomes stubborn and perverse, frequently giving rise to clamorous, violent, wicked, and coarse speech that stings others.
What is called *mrakṣa* (concealment) has the nature of hiding one's own committed misdeeds out of fear of losing profit and reputation;
its function is to obstruct the absence of concealment and to give rise to remorse and distress.
For one who conceals their transgressions, there will inevitably be subsequent regret and distress,
as they lack peace and security both during the causal stage and at the time of the result.
As for what is called "deceit" (*śāṭhya*), its nature is that of guile and fraud, wherein one falsely displays the appearance of possessing virtuous qualities in order to gain profit and reputation.
Its function is to obstruct non-deception and to serve as the basis for wrong livelihood;
that is to say, because those who are deceitful harbor ulterior motives and frequently manifest unreal matters of wrong livelihood.
As for what is called "sycophancy" (māyā):
It is characterized by a nature of artificiality and crookedness adopted for the purpose of ensnaring others.
Its function is to obstruct the instruction of those who are not deceitful.
Those who are deceitful employ crooked means to ensnare and deceive others, artfully adapting their conduct to suit the occasion.
It is for the purpose of gaining the favor of others, or because one has concealed [one's faults] and is thus incapable of receiving the correct instruction of teachers and friends.
As for what is called "hypocrisy" (*mada*):
its nature is that of being intoxicated with pride through defiled attachment toward one's own flourishing prosperity.
Its function is to obstruct that which serves as the basis for non-deceit and non-defilement;
this is because those who are deceitful and intoxicated give rise to all manner of difficult-to-taint phenomena.
As for what is called "harm":
Its nature is the lack of compassion toward sentient beings and the act of harming them;
its function is to obstruct non-harming and to cause affliction.
This is because one who possesses harmful intent afflicts others.
As for what is called envy (*īrṣyā*):
it is characterized by a nature of being self-conceited regarding one's own reputation and profit, being unable to endure the prosperity of others, and being jealous and resentful.
Its function is to obstruct non-envy and to give rise to sorrow and distress.
This means that one who is envious feels deep sorrow and distress upon hearing of or seeing the prosperity of others, and thus lacks peace and stability.
As for what is called "miserliness" (mātsarya),
its nature consists of being attached to wealth and the Dharma, being unable to give them away, and being secretive and stingy.
Its function is to obstruct non-stinginess and to cause hoarding.
This means that one who is stingy is necessarily secretive and withholding,
for they cannot relinquish their accumulation of wealth or the Dharma.
Regarding "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*):
its intrinsic nature is to disregard one's own dharma and to treat the virtuous and good with contempt and rejection;
its function is to obstruct the growth of shame and to give rise to unwholesome conduct.
This refers to those who have no regard for their own dharma;
they slight and reject the virtuous and good, feel no shame for their faults and evils,
and because they obstruct a sense of shame, they cause various unwholesome actions to grow.
Regarding "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*):
its nature is to disregard the world's esteem and to be violent and evil;
its function is to obstruct the growth of shame and to give rise to unwholesome conduct.
This refers to those who have no regard for the world;
they honor the violent and evil, feel no shame for their transgressions and faults,
and because they obstruct a sense of shame and remorse, they cause various unwholesome actions to grow.
Not feeling shame for one's faults and evils is the common characteristic of these two [defilements],
because both lack a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
Rejecting what is good and esteeming what is evil is their specific characteristic.
Because lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) arise individually and separately,
at the time of an unwholesome mind, regardless of whatever object it encounters, there is always the sense of slighting and rejecting the wholesome and honoring and esteeming the unwholesome.
Therefore, these two types both pervade all unwholesome minds.

Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) has the nature of being a defilement of the mind characterized by an inability to endure, delight in, or desire [the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha], as well as their actual virtues and capabilities.
Its function is to obstruct pure faith and to serve as a basis for indolence (*kausīdya*).
This means that those who lack faith are generally characterized by indolence.
One should understand that the three characteristics of non-faith are the opposites of faith:
they consist of a lack of acceptance, a lack of delight, and a lack of aspiration toward what is real, virtuous, and capable.
Furthermore, regarding other matters, there is wrong acceptance, delight, and desire;
these are its causes and effects, not its intrinsic nature.
As for what is called "laziness":
Its nature is laziness regarding the practice of abandoning unwholesome states and cultivating wholesome ones;
its function is to obstruct diligence and increase defilement,
for in one who is indolent, defilements flourish.
To urge others toward defiled matters is also called indolence,
because it causes one to regress from wholesome dharmas.
To urge diligence toward neutral matters is likewise [indolence].
Because there is no advancing or retreating regarding various wholesome and unwholesome states,
this desire and resolve do not have a separate intrinsic nature.
As for what is called "heedlessness":
Its nature is the inability to guard against or cultivate the defiled and pure categories, resulting in unrestrained indulgence.
Its function is to obstruct heedfulness and serve as a basis for increasing evil and diminishing the wholesome;
that is to say, it consists of middling negligence, as well as greed, hatred, and delusion.
The inability to prevent or cultivate the defiled and purified categories is collectively termed heedlessness (*pramāda*);
it possesses no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As for "torpor" (*styāna*),
its nature is to render the mind incapable of functioning with respect to its object;
its function is to obstruct pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
This means that because its intrinsic nature is dullness and heaviness,
it renders the co-arising factors unserviceable.
As for the distinction between this [dullness] and delusion (*moha*):
This means that delusion (*moha*) has the nature of being bewildered and obscured regarding its object;
it is specifically an obstacle to non-delusion (*amoha*), rather than being a state of dullness or heaviness.
As for "restlessness" (*auddhatya*):
Its nature is to cause the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its object;
its function is to obstruct equanimity of application (*upekṣā*) and to serve as an obstacle to calm abiding (*śamatha*).
This is because, by its very nature, it is agitated and restless.
Because it causes co-arising dharmas to be non-quiescent.

As for "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*), its nature is the inability to clearly remember objects of focus; its function is to obstruct right mindfulness and to serve as the basis for distraction.
This refers to "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*).
Because the mind is distracted, delusion causes one to lose mindfulness; therefore, it is called "loss of mindfulness.
Consequently, its intrinsic nature consists of delusion and mindfulness.
Lack of correct awareness (asaṃprajanya) has the nature of erroneous understanding regarding the object under observation;
