its function is to obstruct correct awareness and lead to transgressions.
This means that because those who lack correct awareness (*asamprajanya*) transgress many precepts, "awareness" (*jñāna*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*).
That is to say, due to delusion (*moha*), one's awareness becomes incorrect; this is termed "lack of correct awareness."
Therefore, ignorance and wisdom are combined to constitute its intrinsic nature.
What is called "mental distraction" is precisely "scattering."
Its nature is to cause the mind to wander among various objects of focus.
Its function is to obstruct right concentration and to serve as a basis for unwholesome wisdom;
that is to say, by its very nature of distraction, it agitates and disturbs the mind.
Because it causes all co-arising dharmas to become dissipated.
Its distinction from *auddhatya* (restlessness) is that the latter makes them easily understood.
This causes the object of focus to shift easily.
When the mind is afflicted, due to the power of restlessness, it should constantly shift its understanding and its object from moment to moment;
although there is no shifting of the understanding and the object within a single kṣaṇa.
However, because there is the sense of change within the continuum,
if it is restrained by the power of mindfulness and so forth,
it is like tethering a monkey.
Because there are times when they abide in association [with other afflictions],
restlessness (*auddhatya*) and agitation (*vikṣepa*) both pervade all defiled minds.
As for why only twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are taught:
This means that it is not an affliction (*kleśa*) because it is merely a defiled gross state;
it is either another defiled phenomenon, a particular state (*avasthā*) of this [affliction],
or its outflow (*niṣyanda*).
All are subsumed within these;
they should be understood according to their respective categories as appropriate.
Thus, among the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),...
Among the ten minor [defilements] and the three higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), these are nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

That is to say, among the ten minor ones, anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*mrakṣa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) all have a portion of hatred (*pratigha*) as their essential nature;
for apart from hatred, there are no distinct five characteristics or functions.
The two factors of conceit (*māna*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*) are both subsumed under the category of greed (*lobha*),
because apart from greed, they possess no distinct characteristics or functions.
The three factors of guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) all have as their nature a portion of greed and delusion (*moha*).
If one is free from greed and delusion, there is no occurrence of the three characteristics of guile (*māyā*), deceit (*śāṭhya*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Regarding the three conventional designations within the [five] hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*):
these refer to negligence (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).
Because they conform to other categories,
the two intermediate [elements] and the five great [elements] are all substantially existent;
they possess their own distinct intrinsic natures and do not belong to other categories.
The ten minor [mental factors] do not occur simultaneously with one another,
because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and intense, and each functions as a primary factor.
The two intermediate [mental factors] are associated with all unwholesome minds.
Accordingly, both the minor and major [mental factors] may arise together.
Since it is already admitted that the eight major universal factors arise in defiled minds,
it follows that they can all arise in succession within the minor [factors].
Therefore, the five intermediate [mental factors] are associated with the five feelings;
the ten minor [factors] are indeterminate; the five factors beginning with anger are associated with four [feelings], excluding pleasure;
and the five factors beginning with guile may be associated with all five feelings.
They may all arise simultaneously with the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-pratiniyata-ālambana*),
because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not contradict one another,
and because these five object-specific factors are compatible with all three moral natures.
The two middle [categories] of the eight great [afflictions] are associated with [other] afflictions;
the ten minor ones certainly do not arise together with views or doubt,
as their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse.
Because it is subtle, those five factors—
anger and the rest— are compatible with pride and delusion, but not with greed or hatred;
for all of them are subdivisions of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Avarice, delusion, and pride are neither associated with greed nor with hatred;
they are all subdivisions of greed.
Arrogance is associated exclusively with delusion.
They differ from pride (*māna*) because they are subdivisions of craving (*rāga*). Concealment (*mrakṣa*),
deceit (*śāṭhya*), and guile (*māyā*) are associated with craving, delusion (*moha*), and pride.
Because their modes of activity do not conflict with greed or delusion,
two among the seven minor [unwholesome] factors are categorized exclusively as unwholesome;
the three major [unwholesome] factors and eight among the minor ones also pertain to the indeterminate.
The seven minor [afflictions] and the two middling ones are subsumed solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) and guile (*māyā*) pertain to both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*);
the remaining ones pervade all three realms (*traidhātuka*).
The twenty [types of mind] are all neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
these are exclusively defiled,
whereas those are exclusively pure.
All of these are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation,
because they arise according to the power of the two types of afflictions. Furthermore,
these can also be categorized as general or specific, and as direct or indirect, in their delusion regarding the principles of the truths.
Because all [defilements] arise based on delusion regarding the truths.
The meaning of the remaining categories of phenomena should be clarified as explained in the treatise.
Treatise:
The four indeterminate factors are: first, sleep; second, regret; third, vitarka; and fourth, vicāra.
The commentary states: "This is the sixth category, the four indeterminate factors, because they are not fixed with respect to the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth."
Because they do not necessarily pervade the mind like contact and other factors,
nor do they necessarily pervade the ground like desire and other factors,
these four are established as "indeterminate" (aniyata).
In the *Abhidharmakośa*, greed, anger, pride, and doubt are further added;
this is because the mental factors associated with the various stages of the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) across all levels are not fixed.
Regarding "sleep" (*middha*):
Its nature is a lack of self-mastery and a state of mental obscurity and contraction;
its function is to obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*).
That is to say, in the state of sleep, the body lacks self-mastery.
Because the mind is extremely dull and inferior, functioning through only a single door,
it is distinguished as being "obscured" when in meditative concentration;
this is a brief distinction from the state of wakefulness.
This serves to demonstrate that sleep is not devoid of essence or function;
this name is provisionally established for states of mindlessness,
because it is associated with the mind just like other hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and fetters (paryavasthāna).
Regarding "bad conduct" (kaukṛtya):
its nature is the regret over actions performed;
its function is to obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*).
Bad conduct (*kaukṛtya*) and regret (*vipratisāra*) serve as cause and effect for one another;
for one first performs an action that is ill-done and only subsequently feels remorse.
Thus, it is from bad conduct that regret arises.
Regretting what was not previously done is also subsumed under *kaukṛtya* (remorse).
For example, as when one says in regret: "I previously did not perform such an undertaking;
this is my *kaukṛtya*. Thus, it is because of regret that there is *kaukṛtya*.
Vitarka (applied thought) means seeking;
its nature is to cause the mind to operate coarsely and with urgency toward the objects of mental discourse.
Vicāra (sustained thought) means examining.
It causes the mind to be hurried and its nature consists in the subtle transformation within the sphere of mental verbalization.
Both of these have as their function serving as the basis for the states of physical and mental stability or instability.
It takes a portion of the wisdom of reflection as its essence;
this is because there is a distinction in meaning between not deeply investigating and deeply investigating the objects of mental discourse.
Among these four, vitarka and vicāra are definitely nominally existent (prajñaptisat),
because they are merely composites of volition (cetanā) and wisdom (prajñā) and lack a separate substantial entity.
Drowsiness (middha) and regret (kaukṛtya) are definitely substantially existent (dravyasat).
Because their modes of activity differ from those of other mental factors,
vitarka and vicāra do not correspond with one another;
yet, they are identical in their essential nature.
Because they differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety,
both are capable of being associated with the former two;
the former two are likewise capable of being associated with each other.
The four [mental factors] are all capable of being associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*),
because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can coexist with the five feelings.
The four are all capable of being associated with the five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).
Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) are not mutually contradictory,
sleep can coexist only with the ten wholesome [mental factors].
This occurs solely in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as there is no pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) there.
Vitarka and vicāra may coexist with the eleven wholesome factors,
because they are associated with pliancy (praśrabdhi) within the first dhyāna.
Kaukṛtya may be associated with ignorance (avidyā).
This aspect is coarse,
whereas greed and the others are subtle;
sleep, vitarka, and vicāra coexist with all ten afflictions.
Because these and those are mutually non-contradictory,
remorse (kaukṛtya) is associated with the secondary derivative afflictions (upakleśa),
rather than with the ten [primary] afflictions such as anger (krodha) and so forth, because each of those [ten] has its own distinct basis.
Sleep, vitarka, and vicāra may all coexist in twenty ways,
because they all arise as defiled within states such as sleep and so forth.
These four are all pervasive across the three natures— wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
Because one also feels regret regarding neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma,
it can be associated with both types of wholesome states;
for regret occurs during stages such as hearing the Dharma and so forth.
The remaining three are all associated with both defiled and non-defiled neutral states; however,
*kaukṛtya* (remorse) is not defiled,
because it is understood to be coarse and intense.
Among the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*) exists only in the two intermediate ones.
This is because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse and intense, and it is not the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Sleep (*middha*) excludes the fourth [neutral state], as it is not induced by concentration.
Because the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) can also possess sleep; furthermore,
with the exception of the first [dhyāna], its understanding is weak and subtle,
such that it cannot investigate names, meanings, and so forth.
Regret and sleep exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Vitarka and vicāra exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
this is because the factors of the remaining realms and stages are all sublime and pure.
Regret is not of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
because it is abandoned through the relinquishing of desire.
Sleep, vitarka, and vicāra all pertain to all three types.
Because all conditioned wholesome dharmas are termed "training" (*śaikṣa*) for those seeking liberation,
and all conditioned wholesome dharmas are "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) for those who have reached the culmination of training;
remorse and torpor are exclusively abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, because they arise through the power of wrong views and the like,
and are not directly induced by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),
although vitarka and vicāra are not themselves the true untainted path.
Furthermore, because they can induce that [state] and are themselves induced from it,
they pertain to both the paths of seeing and cultivation and are not included among those to be abandoned;
for these very vitarka and vicāra are themselves not to be abandoned.
Among the five dharmas, two types are encompassed:
vitarka and vicāra, because they are the seven kinds of discrimination;
and right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa), because it is said to be untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it is said that those [subsequent cognitions] are the causes of verbal expression;
because subsequent wisdom preaches the Dharma with vitarka and vicāra,
unlike the Buddha-ground which is effortless (*anābhoga*).
Therefore, these vitarka and vicāra also pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The meanings of the other categories are explained extensively in the treatise.
Such are the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) across these six stages.
It does not mean that it is merely a distinction within the states of the mind itself,
because [the dependent nature] is associated with other-nature (parabhāva) and is not its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Otherwise, the nature of the five aggregates would fail to be established.
Because there is no separate essence for the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations,
yet feeling and perception are established as distinct aggregates,
it is because they are the roots of dispute and the sequential causes of birth and death.
All the remaining [factors] are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*),
and they are also all included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
This is because these three are broad and pervasive enough to encompass everything.
Because all other [phenomena] not included elsewhere are subsumed within this, the treatise states:
"Third, material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are briefly of eleven kinds. Kai says:
The preceding section clarified the mental factors (caitta).
Next, the material phenomena (rūpadharma) will be clarified.
This consists of two parts.
First, the number is stated in general;
subsequently, the items are listed individually according to that number.
This is the first [section].
However, regarding the breadth or narrowness of the names and categories for these material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),
there are differences in what is taught in the treatises of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
For instance, the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states that there are two kinds.
First are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*),
namely earth, water, fire, and wind as commonly explained.
They are called "great" because their substance is vast, their characteristics are predominant, and they give rise to great functional activities.
Because it serves as the basis for other forms and is capable of producing them, it is called a "seed" (*bīja*).
Second are the derived forms produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*),
namely all forms, odors, tastes, and so forth.
That which arises based on the aforementioned four great elements and is produced by them is called derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
The eleven kinds of matter mentioned herein are such derived matter.
This refers to matter derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Even if non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) exists, it too is derived from the four great elements,
because it is of a derivative nature.
However, whenever that which is derived is mentioned, its creator must necessarily be implied;
thus, it is not contradictory for them to be indicated through mutual abbreviation.
This refers to derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the refutation of the Hīnayāna is generally divided into two parts:
first, those that are resistant (*sapratigha*) and composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The second is non-obstructive;
it is not composed of atoms.
The ten types mentioned previously are obstructive forms.
Because these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*),
whereas the latter kind [of derived matter] is non-resistant (*apratigha*) matter;
although it is produced by the great elements, it is not composed of atoms.
This "possessing resistance" (sapratigha) has the meaning of "obstruction.
In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is explained that there are two meanings:
first, the sense of physical obstruction.
It is like a hand obstructing a hand or a stone obstructing a stone;
these are the two meanings of "obstruction" (*pratighāta*),
because the subject that grasps an object is obstructed by that very object which serves as its sphere of perception.
Furthermore, this obstruction is of two kinds.
First is objective obstruction (*viṣayapratighāta*),
which consists of the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, a portion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and various mental factors (*caitta*) among the eighteen realms.
These thirteen elements (dhātus) are called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*) because their nature is to grasp objects and they are constrained by those objects.
Second, there is "resistance regarding the object of cognition" (*ālambana-pratighāta*).
Among the eighteen elements, only the seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*) and the mental factors (*caitta*) within the dharma-element arise in dependence upon objects.
They are called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*) because they arise only when the objective field (*viṣaya*) acts as a powerful condition; that is,
the faculties and consciousnesses are constrained by their respective objects,
and they do not function toward anything else beyond those limits.
In this context, there is no resistance through an object (*ālambana-pratighāta*),
because mind and mental factors do not depend upon an external object in that manner.
Furthermore, regarding the five categories of the Abhidharma, based on the eleven types of matter, they are briefly summarized as three.
First, there is that which is visible and resistant;
this refers to the initial category of the object-field of form,
because it is a dharma that is visible and possesses resistance.
The second category consists of those that are invisible but possess resistance;
this refers to the subsequent nine types,
as they are all not visible yet are obstructive.
Three are invisible and non-obstructive;
this refers to the last type of form,
because it is both invisible and without resistance.
Furthermore, that same treatise explains four kinds of matter:
first, that which is born of maturation;
second, that which is nurtured by growth.
Third, the outflowing (niṣyanda);
fourth, the momentary (kṣaṇika).
Fearing prolixity, I shall not explain them further.
The *Lèzhě* (The Joyful One) explains this:
"As for the statement that there are two or twenty types of form (*rūpa*),
these are subsumed under this sixth category of distinct forms."
As will be explained below,
there is no need for further elaboration here.
Treatise:

1. The eye; 2. the ear; 3. the nose; 4. the tongue; 5. the body; 6. visible forms; 7. sounds; 8. odors; 9. tastes; 10. tangibles; 11. matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Kai said:
This is presented here according to the specific headings and listings.
This extensive explanation does not appear in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*;
it is now clarified based on the intended meaning as explained in various treatises.
However, there are three distinct meanings in the explanation of this text:
first, the explanation of its general name;
second, the specific names within the general [category].
Regarding the specific names within the three categories:
as for the initial general name,
the first five types are the sense-faculties (indriya) based on matter (rūpa).
The former five kinds are the material forms that are objective spheres (*viṣaya-rūpa*);
the latter one kind is non-resistant matter (*apratigha-rūpa*).
"Superior production" is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*).
All of these have the four great elements as their pure nature,
for they function like precious jewels by emitting light.
Although they are all termed "form" (rūpa), they are not apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Its existence is inferred by the fact that it can give rise to consciousness;
although the eighth consciousness and the wisdom of a Tathāgata are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
they are not obtained through the direct perception of other forms of cognition or consciousness.
Because it is not commonly known in the world,
its existence is inferred based on the arising of consciousness;
this is for the purpose of making the apprehension of objects clear and distinct.
Although the eyes, ears, and noses each arise in two locations,
they are established as a single faculty because their substance and category are identical.
Because the objects and their corresponding consciousnesses are subsumed within a single *dhātu*,
and because their functions differ in terms of range, speed, and clarity,
the eye, ear, and so forth are taught in this sequential order.
Next, the term "object" (*viṣaya*) carries the meaning of that which is observed;
this simultaneously encompasses both the defiled and the pure senses.
If one uses the term "dust" (*rajas*), it refers specifically to the defiled sense.
Because it is defiled by objects (*viṣaya*), it is called an "object.
The matter of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) is likewise included within the category of objects.
If this is so, why is it alone designated as "matter" (*rūpa*) at the outset?
The answer has two meanings.
First, it is by way of distinction;
for all others have their own distinct names.
Second, by way of being preeminent:
although all are termed "form" (rūpa),
this is so because it is the most preeminent.
Therefore, although the objects of form are distinct, they receive a collective name based on the sequential function of the sense organs that apprehend them;
the same applies to the sequence of visible forms, sounds, odors, and so forth.
The general explanation of the name is concluded.
To explain the specific names,

I shall now provide an interpretation based on the common principles found in treatises such as the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the Abhidharma works of the Hīnayāna.
There are pure atoms (paramāṇu) distributed upon the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya),
abiding in opposition to their objects like a *campaka* flower.
In Sanskrit, this is specifically named *kṛcchra*.
*Kṛ* has the meaning of "action," while *cchra* has the meaning of "emptiness."
This means that because it functions within emptiness to clearly illuminate form,
it is called "eye" (*cakṣus*) by way of its derivative etymology;
for the eye possesses this function of illuminating within emptiness.
There are pure atoms within the ear canal that abide in a circular arrangement like a rolled birch bark;
it is here that sound repeatedly arrives and can be heard.
Therefore, in the Sanskrit language it is called *śrotra*.
*Śrotra* here means "that which can hear.
In its secondary sense, it is translated separately as "the ear."
Because the ear possesses this faculty of hearing,
there are pure atoms (*paramāṇu*) located within the nasal bridge,
on the back of which they face downward like a pair of fingernails.
Because of this, it is able to smell odors;
for this reason, in the Sanskrit language it is called *ghrāṇa*.
*Ghrāṇa* means "that which can smell."
According to another interpretation,
it is translated as "nose," because the nose possesses this function of smelling.
There are pure atoms (*paramāṇu*) distributed upon the tongue.
Its shape is like a half-moon.
It is capable of tasting flavors and can eliminate hunger and emaciation.
It frequently utters speech to manifest and summon.
Therefore, in the Sanskrit language it is called *jihvā*.
*Jihvā* here means "that which can taste.
As for its secondary meaning, it is translated differently as "tongue."
Because the tongue possesses this capacity for tasting,
there exist pure atoms (*paramāṇu*) throughout all parts of the body;
these follow the various sense organs and are accumulated everywhere, enabling the experience of various tactile sensations.
Therefore, in the Sanskrit language it is called *kāya*.
In this land [of China], *kāya* is translated as "accumulation.
That which is here called "body" (*shen*) carries the meaning of an "assemblage."
In this context, it is translated separately as "body" (kāya).
As for "form" (rūpa), it refers to that which manifests in a specific location and whose substantial quality can be increased;
thus it is designated separately as "form."
These specific names for colors are further twenty-five:
those of the emerald-green class are called "blue" (nīla);
those of the crimson-bright class are called "yellow" (pīta).
Substances such as vermilion are termed "red";
those of a pure and pristine nature are called "white";
and that which spreads its flames to illuminate everything is collectively named "light."
When light is obstructed, it produces an image; when a defiled shadow produces light, it manifests itself as clarity.
When the essence is dull and lacking illumination, it is called darkness (*tamas*).
When firewood burns and vapor rises, it is named smoke (*dhūma*).
The breath of the dragon’s roar is called cloud;
light soil wafting through the air is dust;
when the vapors of earth and water ascend, they become mist.
When the form of an object is elongated and straight, it is called "long.
When the appearance of an object is cramped and confined, it is named "short.
When the essential characteristics of a substance are raised upward, it is named "high."
When things are sunken and withered, they are called "low";
when the six sides are level and upright, they are called "square";
and when the four corners are worn and rounded, they are called "round."
That which is broad at the sides is called coarse;
that which is thin and elongated from top to bottom is called fine.
Alternatively, one may distinguish between coarse and fine based on their quality, whether good or bad.
The upright and central abiding is called "correct";
being partial, biased, slanted, or curved is called "incorrect.
Wandering through vacuities and dust is termed "remote form."
Bodily actions such as bending and so forth are called manifest color (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
That which is perceived within empty space is called the color of uniform space (*ākāśaikavarṇa-rūpa*).
These first four types of color are self-evident by their very nature.
Because it does not depend on others for its establishment, it is substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
The remaining twenty-one exist as states (*avasthā*) of the first four types of matter;
they are all conceptually designated (*prajñaptisat*).
The two and twenty [types of matter] established in the *Abhidharmakośa* lack coarse or subtle matter,
because they are subsumed under length and shortness.
The latter three types do not exist,
because they are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Neither the Mahāyāna nor the Hīnayāna sūtras or śāstras mention black [as a color].
Alternatively, it is included within the blue because it is proximate to blue;
or it follows the lotus, which has only four colors.
Alternatively, because it is not distinct in essence from dark color,
the frequent disputes and refutations regarding its increase and decrease have led to divergent theories.
It is called "sound" (*śabda*) because it manifests names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*).
This sound has eleven distinct types.
The first is sound produced from great elements that are appropriated by causes;
this refers to that which arises from sentient beings.
Sentient beings are those whose great elements and sounds are appropriated by consciousness;
these two causes are not appropriated when they arise from that which is non-sentient.
Because non-sentient things are not appropriated by consciousness,
the sound [of the term "sound"] possesses all three causes;
that is to say, it is produced by both sentient and non-sentient beings together.
It arises from great elements that are not appropriated (*anupātta*).
Fourth are agreeable sounds (*manojña-śabda*),
which are those that accord with one's desires and gladden the mind.
There are five kinds of unpleasant sounds, which are sounds that one hears and finds disagreeable;
that is to say, whatever is loathsome and displeasing to one.
Sixth is the discordant sound, which refers to a sound that is heard as being neither pleasant nor unpleasant,
such as when one feels pleasure even while being reviled or insulted.
Because it is merely equal within the consciousness of the hearer,
it is a sound established by common consensus throughout the seven generations;
that is, that which arises from what is conventionally established as verbal instruction in the world.
Such as carts, houses, and so forth;
these are sounds produced by the eightfold [path] and are those arising from the attainment of the untainted (anāsrava) by the noble ones (ārya).
Because the substance of the noble teachings of the Three Piṭakas is established upon this sound,
there is ninth, the sound of the thoroughly imagined,
which refers to the verbal instructions originated by various non-Buddhist outsiders.
Because it arises from what is conceptually grasped as false,
the sound subsumed under the ten noble expressions arises based on the four kinds of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Because there are eight kinds of true speech,
the eleven types of sounds subsumed under non-noble speech also arise based on the fourfold [categories] of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Because there are eight kinds of false speech,
the first three types of sound may be considered substantially existent,
for they are established based on sounds that possess substantial reality.
The remaining eight kinds of sound are all established as conventional designations,
for they are spoken of in terms of the various states of the first three sounds.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* speaks of eight kinds.
However, because they are established as "agreeable" or "disagreeable" based on whether they are appropriated or not, and whether they are sentient or insentient, there are only that many [types].
Departing from their substance and concealing their form, they frequently shift with the wind.
That which is smelled by the nose is specifically termed "fragrance" (*gandha*);
this term also applies to odors that are foul.
It is not only agallochum and musk that are uniquely called "fragrance.
For this reason, this fragrance has six distinct names;
the first is "excellent fragrance" (*sugandha*).
Fragrances that are beneficial to the faculties and agreeable to the mind—such as those from aloeswood and sandalwood—which may be taken with pleasure, are collectively termed "good fragrances.
This is because substances such as aloeswood and sandalwood do not accord with the minds of all sentient beings.
Second are "bad fragrances."
Odors that impair the sense faculties, contradict one's feelings, or are not taken up by the nose as pleasant are all termed "unwholesome" (akuśala).
This is because things such as excrement and filth do not equally cause impairment for all sentient beings.
Third are neutral odors (sama-gandha).
It is neither harmful nor beneficial, neither conformable nor contrary, and because it is not called "increase" even when desirable, it is termed "equanimity.
Fourth is the co-arising fragrance,
which means it arises simultaneously with its primary substance.
Just as with aloeswood and other substances, because their material qualities coexist,
there is the "fragrance of the fivefold combination," meaning that various substances are mixed together to form a single fragrance.
Because this fragrance arises differently from others, it is called the sixth:
the fragrance of transformation.
This refers to the fragrance that arises according to the time when substances are combined.
However, because this fragrance undergoes transformation,
the former three are real, as they constitute the fundamental substance of fragrance.
The latter three are provisional,
as they are established through transformation.
If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it speaks of only four types.
These are what are called the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the neutral.
The latter two are established based on the benefit or harm to the sense faculties;
since they do not constitute separate entities, they are not explained separately.
Depending on the presence or absence of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), they repeatedly bring about gross suffering through their impairment or benefit of the sense faculties;
this is specifically termed "taste" (*rasa*).
Furthermore, there are twelve distinct varieties of this taste.
First, bitter;
second, sour;
third, sweet.
Fourth, pungent;
fifth, salty;
sixth, bland.
These six tastes constitute its actual substance;
this is universally known in the world and requires no further explanation.
Seventh is the "taste of being savored."
This refers to that which accords with one's preferences and is agreeable to the mind.
The eight disagreeable objects refer to that which accords with what one dislikes and is not agreeable to the mind.
Ninth is the discordant taste,
meaning it is neither pleasant nor unpleasant but merely neutral.
Tenth is the co-emergent taste.
This means that because both the flavor and the substance coexist within the fruit,
there is an "elevenfold combination of flavors," as the various substances are mixed together yet produced distinctly.
Twelfth is the taste of transformation (*vipariṇāma-rasa*).
This refers to the transformation of taste according to the degree of ripeness of the substance;
these six are conventional (*prajñapti*).
Because they are established based on the six preceding higher stages (*ūrdhva-bhāga*),
the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* mentions only six types;
these are precisely the substantial entities of the aforementioned six flavors.
That which arises according to the objects and is grasped by the body,
causing benefit or harm to the sense faculties,
is specifically termed "contact" (sparśa). This contact has twenty-two specific varieties.

Roughness, smoothness, lightness, heaviness, slowness, quickness, cold, warmth, hunger, thirst, satiety, oppression, strength, weakness, itching, pain, old age, death, fatigue, respiration, stickiness, and vigor.
In the Abhidharma, the sequence differs from this.
Furthermore, "strength" and "weakness" are merely changes in name for what is superior and inferior.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, four additional types are added, namely the four great elements: solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.
Because all [sensations] are able to have contact within the body;
because it is the substantial basis for the aforementioned various contacts;
and because the various contacts are established based on its states.
Including lightness, heaviness, roughness, smoothness, hunger, thirst, and cold,
these together constitute the eleven tangibles;
others are not mentioned.
Because its meaning is not fully established,
there is no substantial entity to serve as a counterpart;
it is not apprehended by the five sense faculties.
That which is perceived solely by the mental faculty (*manas*) is called "form included within the sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa*).
"Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to that which provides a norm and sustains its own characteristic.
Regarding "own-characteristics," "common characteristics," and so forth:
"place" (sthāna) refers to a location,
specifically the locus that serves as the object of the mind.
Because this form is subsumed under this sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana),
it is specifically termed "form subsumed under the sphere of phenomena" (dharmāyatanasaṃgṛhītarūpa).
Furthermore, there are five distinct types of this form.
First, the most abbreviated form of matter is also called the atom (*paramāṇu*);
its ancient name was the "limitless" (*anu*).
It is also called "subtle atom" (*paramāṇu*).
By abbreviating those coarse forms down to their ultimate limit, one reaches the subtle atom;
that which is adjacent to empty space is called "extremely abbreviated form."
This is not seen by the eye, but is an object of mental focus;
that is to say, the practitioner of yoga, by means of conceptual wisdom,
gradually deconstructs coarse material forms.
When it reaches the point where it can no longer be divided from its adjacent space,
it is designated as an "extreme atom" (paramāṇu).
If one were to divide it further, it would appear as mere emptiness.
It is not called "form" [in the ordinary sense].
Because it is a concise designation for atoms, it is called "extremely concise form" (*paramāṇu-saṃkṣepa-rūpa*).
Second is "extremely remote form" (*parama-vivikta-rūpa*).
That is to say, the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the ultimate limit of form (*rūpa*).
Since it possesses no spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*),
it is devoid of any other obstructive contact.
Because it is extremely remote and isolated, it is called "extremely remote color" (*paramāṇu-rūpa*).
Although this is not different from "extremely condensed [color]" (*paramāṇu-saṃhata*) in terms of its essential substance,
their meanings differ.
Therefore, it is categorized separately:
the form derived from the three types of sensation arises from evil thoughts,
vows, and oaths prompted by evil friends, whereby one undergoes various acts of non-restraint.

Furthermore, there is the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) produced by these two: [the restraint arising from] the vows of renunciation and the distinct restraints of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) undertaken through virtuous friends and the arousal of wholesome thoughts and aspirations.
Although these are established based on the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions and aspirations, [they are nonetheless designated as such].
Because it arises from matter and also serves to prevent matter,
it is therefore called "matter derived by feeling" (*vedanā-samādatta-rūpa*).
Fourth is "matter produced by conceptual construction" (*parikalpita-rūpa*).
This refers to the form of the self and phenomena as grasped by the imputing mind as being real;
this lacks an underlying essence and possesses only an image that appears resembling the characteristics of form.
If the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) arising from the mental consciousness— which functions simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses— takes objective form (rūpa) as its object,
it is a "real object" (svabhāva-viṣaya) and is therefore not subsumed under this [category of] form.
Because it is the image-aspect of the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
it is called "form arising from universal conceptualization" (*parikalpita-rūpa*).
Fifth is "form produced by mastery."
The sovereign bodhisattvas, great śrāvakas,
and ordinary persons who possess mastery over meditative concentration,
by means of sequential meditative absorption, produce the various aspects of color— such as blue, yellow, red, and so forth— that are transformed through their contemplation of blue and other colors.
Alternatively, the eighth consciousness transforms the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five sense-objects into forms such as gold, silver, ghee, or milk;
because these are newly produced through the power of mastery (*vaśitā*),
they are called "matter produced by mastery" (*vaśitā-nirmita-rūpa*).
The first four are conventional,
because they are established as mere designations based solely upon the observation of mind and so forth;
the last one is entirely real.
Furthermore, because it is also the object-condition (*ālambana-viṣaya*) of the eighth consciousness,
the Sarvāstivādins of the Hīnayāna all assert that it is substantially real (*dravyasat*).
However, regarding the matter-form included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), they speak of only one kind.
This refers precisely to the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by wholesome or unwholesome [actions];
it refers to what is here termed "matter derived from feeling" (vedanā-samgṛhīta-rūpa),
and no other [matter] is mentioned.
Because the meaning is not complete.
These eleven kinds of matter thus described are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*) according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Apart from the mind, there exist [objects] separately;
yet, according to the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra*, all these are the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
Depending on their respective magnitude, they manifest instantaneously as a single appearance.
It is not that they are formed into a single entity by the combination of atoms;
rather, they are all subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) among the five aggregates,
because they all possess the nature of being accumulated and subject to transformation and resistance.
It is subsumed within eleven of the twelve bases (*āyatana*),
because they possess the sense of being gateways for the arising [of consciousness] as appropriate; it is not,
however, the mind-faculty (*manas*).
Because it is not mind-consciousness,
it is subsumed within eleven of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
as its meaning is that of the fundamental source capable of producing [them].
Since the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana),
and elements (dhātu) pertain to both the states of cause and effect, they also pertain to the state of Buddhahood. Some say:
Because the Buddha possesses the physical sense faculties and their objects,
and because the teaching that he lacks the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
his nature in the state of fruition is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because the aggregates and so forth of the Buddha’s body are all wondrously pure,
the pure consciousness that undergoes transformation is not outflowing (*sāsrava*);
those who speak of it as being outflowing do so in accordance with the Hīnayāna.
If it exists in the causal stage, its nature is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
because it is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
and because that transforming consciousness is itself contaminated.
Because the nature and category of the seeing-part and the perceived-part are identical,
if the nature of untainted form is exclusively wholesome,
it is because all such forms are truly beneficial dharmas.
If there are contaminated forms (*rūpa*), their nature is entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is because the consciousness that undergoes transformation is itself indeterminate in nature,
and because the treatises state that visible form and sound are neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
If the matter within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana-rūpa) is indeterminate as to its existence or non-existence:
if it exists within the body of a Buddha, it is not matter of conceptual construction (parikalpita-rūpa),
because all Buddhas have already severed the mind of clinging to conceptual constructions.
Although the most concise and remote forms of color are likewise non-existent in reality,
they nonetheless exist as conceptual constructs according to worldly convention, because there is a wisdom of conceptualization that follows such conventions,
and because the Buddhas universally take both conventional and ultimate phenomena as their objects of cognition.
The Buddha constantly gives rise to all virtuous thoughts and aspirations;
because his precepts are never severed from all forms,
he attains great mastery and is able to effect all transformations.
Because that sovereign form definitely exists,
if one is in the stage of a cause, the noble ones of the three vehicles will possess all five types according to their respective positions.
Because conceptual grasping arises during moments of mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
the four [types of mind] should all be understood accordingly. Furthermore,
when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) attain a concentrated mind, there are likewise five types.
For those who have not yet attained meditative concentration, there may still be the pervasive conceptualization of matter derived from volition;
this is because the mind of conceptual attachment is constantly uninterrupted,
and wholesome or unwholesome intentions and aspirations arise alternately in accordance with it.
The first two types of matter are categorized exclusively as wholesome,
because they arise solely from a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*).
Matter derived from moral precepts (*vijñapti-rūpa*) pertains to both wholesome and unwholesome natures.
Because it is produced by wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral volitions,
the form arising from pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita) permeates all three natures;
this is because it is an object consisting solely of mental images (pratibimba) derived from the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga).
The nature of the forms produced by mastery is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because they are transformations of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that result from supernormal powers (*ṛddhiphala*).
The principles regarding their realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and so forth, should be reflected upon according to reason.
Treatise:
The fourth category, the formations dissociated from mind, consists of twenty-four types.
Commentary: Next, the fourth category, the formations dissociated from mind, is explained.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general presentation stating the number;
second, a detailed enumeration according to that number.
This is the first [category].
According to the Hīnayāna school, there are fourteen;
there are also those who further add the characteristics of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Now, the Mahāyāna school asserts twenty-four [factors].
If the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* follows its refutation of the Hīnayāna schools,
it merely reveals fourteen factors that are dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
If works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* manifest the tenets of the Mahāyāna and analyze twenty-four meanings of non-association (*viprayukta*),
then it is because such works as the *Yogācārabhūmi* possess extensive analytical distinctions.

This is now based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and other treatises such as those on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). The treatise lists twenty-four [factors]:

(1) acquisition (*prāpti*), (2) life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), (3) generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*), (4) the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), (5) the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), (6) the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), (7) the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), (8) the group of names (*nāma-kāya*), (9) the group of phrases (*pada-kāya*), (10) the group of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), (11) birth (*jāti*), (12) aging (*jarā*), (13) duration (*sthiti*), (14) impermanence (*anityatā*), (15) transmigration (*pravṛtti*), (16) specific determination (*pratiniyama*), (17) association (*samyoga*), (18) rapidity (*java*), (19) sequence (*anukrama*), (20) spatial direction (*deśa*), (21) time (*kāla*), (22) number (*saṃkhyā*), (23) the nature of conjunction (*sāmagrī*), and (24) the nature of non-conjunction (*asāmagrī*). The commentary states: "To open [the meaning]: [it is as follows].
This is an enumeration based on number.
As for the term "attainment" (prāpti),
it carries the meaning of "accomplishment" (siddhi).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the commentary on the meaning states:
"With respect to those dharmas that can be accomplished by sentient beings,
that which is first acquired and not lost is termed 'acquisition' (*prāpti*)."
This attainment of accomplishment is of three kinds.
The first is the accomplishment of seeds,
which pertains to afflicted phenomena, various neutral phenomena, and innate wholesome phenomena.
Those that manifest without effort are defiled but have not yet been suppressed by śamatha,
and they are neutral but have not yet been permanently destroyed by the noble path.
If that which is acquired at birth has not been impaired by wrong view,
both its active functioning and its non-functioning are termed "accomplished," because its capacity for activity remains unimpaired and unsubdued.
Second is the accomplishment of mastery.
This refers to those wholesome dharmas produced through application;
a portion of the seeds of the indeterminate are intensified, while the wholesome [seeds] arise from application.
This refers to all mundane and supramundane merits consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Because one attains mastery in practice through these preparatory applications (*prayoga*),
one who accomplishes this virtue is called a "master" (*vaśin*).
Therefore, the wholesome states of preparatory application and so forth are called "accomplishment through mastery.
Third is "accomplishment through manifestation," which refers to the manifestation of the aggregates, bases, and elements as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
If they were severed, damaged, or suppressed, they would certainly not be accomplished;
because they have not been damaged or suppressed, they are all able to manifest.
This very manifestation is what is termed "accomplishment" (samanvāgama).
The former two refer to seeds,
whereas this refers to active manifestation;
therefore, there are three types of accomplishment.
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"It refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as the substance of the destiny of rebirth."
Because it is the pervasive and continuous retribution fruit (*vipākaphala*),
it is able to maintain the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their bases (*āśraya*) so that they do not perish or cease; thus,
it is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*).
The state in which the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) has not yet relinquished its appropriation (upādāna) and has not yet been destroyed is called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
This consciousness arises directly from its own seeds.
Based precisely upon the seeds that directly produce this consciousness,
the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is conventionally established as the determination of the duration of the specific functional capacity induced by karma;
for apart from this life-faculty, [such a determination] cannot be found.
Both the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) analyses apply here.
Regarding "homogeneity" (*nikāyasabhāga*),
according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
"Multitude" (zòng) means many;
"commonality" (tóng) means similarity;
"division" (fèn) refers to the cause.

The "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is so called because it gives rise to identical cognitions and verbal expressions based on the similarity among the various classes of sentient beings' bodies.
Alternatively, "group" (*nikāya*) has the meaning of "class" (*jāti*);
that is to say, it refers to the commonality of classes such as humans, devas, and so forth.
"Commonality of the multitude" (*nikāyasabhāga*) is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
As for "the nature of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*),
it means that all noble ones (*ārya*) are termed "common-born" (*sabhāga*).
Ordinary, ignorant people are called "pṛthagjana" (heterogeneous beings).
Because of the two kinds of obstacles to be abandoned through vision,
these ordinary, ignorant people give rise to divergent views.
They are born into different destinies and born into different species; that is,
they are at the stage where the seeds of the two obstacles have not yet been permanently destroyed.
That which is able to obstruct the Noble Path is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva).
It is the birth of the distinct,
the nature of one who is distinct.
All [these terms] are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds.
Because of this nature, one does not attain the noble dharmas;
therefore, in the Hīnayāna, it is specifically termed "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).
Regarding the concentration on signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*),
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains:
there are certain non-Buddhists who cling to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) as being nirvāṇa.
One regards this perception as a festering ulcer and the like, being the cause of birth and death.
One cultivates this meditative concentration preceded by the mental application (*manasikāra*) of the perception of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*).
This is because, at the time of practicing concentration, one feels revulsion toward the perception [of the object] during the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for that concentration.
One causes this mental image to become gradually subtler and more refined.
At the time when the mind is thus refined, it perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
forming seeds for an extremely predominant mind of revulsion and so forth.
Because the seeds of mental activity and perception have been impaired and suppressed by this,
the non-constant mental activity and perception do not arise;
it is on the basis of this state that this meditative absorption is provisionally established.
The meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is so named because the cessation of perception is its primary characteristic.
Regarding the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
This means that when those of the two vehicles perceive the arising of coarse and fluctuating minds,
they inevitably experience weariness and aversion toward these coarse and fluctuating mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta*); therefore,
they take the mental attention directed toward the perception of cessation as their precursor.

Relying on the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one contemplates the untainted (*anāsrava*) as a preparatory practice (*prayoga*) to enter the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittanirodha*);
this causes the mind and mental factors to become increasingly subtle and minute.
At the time when the mind is most subtle, it perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Having brought about an extremely predominant state of mind characterized by revulsion and so forth,
this power is able to suppress both the constantly active and the occasionally active mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Based on this particular state, this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is conventionally established.
Because this meditative absorption can cause the cessation of all mental states— both those that function constantly and those that do not—
it is called the "attainment of cessation" (nirodhasamāpatti).
As for the "unconscious entity" (asaṃjñisattva):
It is the very substance of the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* refers to it as "maturation.
One enters the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in pursuit of the fruit of no-thought.
Since this meditative absorption is wholesome, its seeds are also wholesome.
These seeds, perfumed by this state, bring about that ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*);
based on this, coarse and mobile perceptions and so forth do not arise.
The name is established based on this state: because during the causal stage,
determinate perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth do not function,
it is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
At the time of fruition, because it does not arise through retribution, perception, and so forth,
it is called a "signless entity" (*animitta-vastu*).
Therefore, the entity and the meditative concentration differ entirely in their essential natures.
The term "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñika*) is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
As for the term "name-body" (*nāmakāya*),
in Sanskrit it is called *naman*.
This is translated as "name" (*nāman*).
It has the meaning of "refuge" (*śaraṇa*),
because it refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena that constitute the object of refuge.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The *Pañcaskandhaka* states:
"A name is a metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*) for the intrinsic nature of all phenomena."
As it is said regarding matters such as the eyes and ears of humans and devas:
if there is only a single name, it is simply called a "name" (nāma);
if it reaches two names, it becomes a "name-group" (nāmakāya).
From three names upward, it is called a "multitude of names" (*nāman-kāya*);
because it is the body (*kāya*) of names, it is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
The subsequent phrases, such as "syllables" (*vyañjana*) and so forth, should be understood accordingly.
Since "body" (kāya) has the meaning of "collection," the term for "phrase-body" (padakāya) is called *pada* in Sanskrit.
This is translated as "traces.
Just as seeing an elephant's tracks indicates the presence of an elephant,
so too do these four lines indicate the existence of verbose textual elaborations.
The term is translated according to its meaning as a constituent of a sentence.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state:
"A 'sentence' (*pada*) is that which expresses a specific meaning."
Regarding the phrase "the five aggregates, etc.":
a phrase (*pada*) is a designation for the differentiation of phenomena (*dharma*),
such as when it is said that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent," and so forth.
While there are five types of phrases, such as those in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are now two types of phrases according to the Mahāyāna:
first, the phrase of the fulfillment of the collection of dharmas; [and second, the phrase of the fulfillment of the collection of meanings].
This should be subsumed under the middle-length sentences of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
One simply collects various names so that they are neither too long nor too short;
when eight characters are complete, they constitute one sentence.

The second is the "phrase that fully manifests the meaning," which encompasses the remaining four phrases of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. This does not merely take the literal words in their entirety without regard for the underlying meaning; rather, it fully reveals the complete significance of the sense.
A "single phrase" (*pada*) is defined as that which, regardless of its variable syllable count—whether short or long—fully expresses a complete meaning;
therefore, there are distinctions between phrases based on their brevity or length, and their position as preceding or following.
As for the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*):
This refers to the syllable itself;
in Sanskrit it is called *vyañjana*,
which is translated here as "phoneme" (*wen*).
This is the formal (scriptural) language.
To say "akṣara" is the vernacular term; it is translated as "letter.
This is the colloquial language.
Fearing that there may be those who do not realize that "text" (*vyañjana*) and "syllable" (*akṣara*) are one and the same,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Text is precisely syllable."
This is precisely that upon which the preceding names and phrases depend;
because names and phrases exist by depending on phonemes (*vyañjana*),
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it serves as the basis for the two.
The ancient translators rendered it as "flavor" (*rasa*).
Because the four dharmas were designated by means of *vyañjana*, their textual form resembled a fan-flavor (*vyajanarasa*).
Due to this similarity in wording, they erroneously translated it as "flavor."
According to the Hīnayāna, each of these possesses its own distinct nature;
that nature is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) and exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
Now, according to our Mahāyāna school, all three of these are merely conventionally established upon sound and possess no separate substantial nature.
If, according to what is expressed, the conventional designation applies to all three natures,
then whatever is spoken of based on those [natures] is identical to sound.
As for that which is called "arising":
This refers to the initial stage at which all phenomena first arise.
The *Pañcaskandhaka* states:
"Birth is the intrinsic nature of that which, within a particular category of sentient beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), was previously non-existent and now comes to be."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Arising manifests the existence of a phenomenon,
because it did not previously exist."
That which is called "aging" (jarā) has the meaning of "alteration" (anyathātva),
for it is the transformation of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) that is designated as aging.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This very continuity, its transformation, is called 'change' (*anyathātva*);
that which is called 'abiding' (*sthiti*)..."
The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states:
"It is the brief pause at the stage of arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts state: [as follows].
That which follows in a similar succession after having arisen is called "abiding.
As for what is termed "impermanence," the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* and other treatises also refer to it as "cessation."
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), having arisen, exist for a moment and then cease;
they are not like unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), which exist eternally,
nor are they like a rabbit’s horns, which exist eternally as non-existent.
Existence is impermanent;
non-existence is not impermanent.
Therefore, conditioned phenomena are called impermanent.
It is not that impermanence is established only in the absence of a state;
for this subsequent non-existence is expressed as the characteristic of cessation.
These ten [characteristics] below are not established by the Hīnayāna.
It is subsumed under these six causes and four conditions; therefore,
it is not mentioned among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*),
nor is it explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the term "transmigration" (*pravṛtti*):
it refers to the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
As the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
This refers to the nature of the uninterrupted continuity of the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
As for "distinctness" (*pratiniyama*),
it means that from beginningless time, the seeds of cause and effect are definitively differentiated and possess no characteristic of confusion or disorder.
Therefore, the *Xiányáng shèngjiào lǜlùn* states:
"It refers to the respective determinate nature of all causes and effects.
As for the term "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*):
This is precisely the non-contradictory nature of cause and effect from beginningless time.
Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā* states:
"The nature of the correspondence between the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)."
Regarding "swift momentum" (*vega*):
it refers to the nature of the rapid flow of the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
This refers to the very nature of the rapid flux of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
As for the term "succession," it signifies that cause and effect do not arise simultaneously.
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"It refers to the sequential nature of each and every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*).
As for what is called 'direction' (*diś*):"
Regarding the limits of form (*rūpa-gocara-pramāṇa*),
the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"It refers to the very nature of the limits of various objective spheres of form."
The Yoga [Śāstra] speaks of three [directions]:
namely, above, below, and across.
As for what is called "time":
There are two meanings:
first, the establishment and manifestation of the distinctions of temporal periods through the power of the rising and setting of the solar orb;
second, the establishment and manifestation of the distinctions of conventional reality through the power of the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
According to this, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are three times:
namely, the past, the future, and the present.
As for what is called "number":
The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states:
"It refers to that which increases in accordance with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to a corresponding degree.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
This refers to the distinct natures of formations (*saṃskāra*)— whether one, ten, a hundred, or a thousand.
Regarding the term "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*),
the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states:
This refers to the occasion when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) come together through conditions.
The *Xianyang* [Shengjiao lun] also states:
"The nature of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is the convergence of conditions."
Regarding "non-concordance" (*asāmagrī*),
the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states:
"It refers to the disjunction between cause and effect among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)."
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"The nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is that their conditions are dissonant;
such are the so-called dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)."
Although there are twenty-four distinct names and categories,
they are collectively established as provisional designations based upon eight stages,
as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, and other treatises.
One type is established according to the states of increase and decrease of the wholesome and unwholesome;
that is to say, it is "attainment" (*prāpti*).
This is a conventional designation established based on the states in which the three natures—form, mind, and mental factors—can be accomplished.
The second category consists solely of those established based on the mind alone, without differentiating its various states;
these are the two meditative attainments and the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).
They are provisionally established because they represent states in which the seeds of the mind are suppressed, causing the sixth and seventh consciousnesses to cease.
Third, one type is established based on the temporal state of the abiding of form and mind;
this refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
It is a provisional designation established based on the maturation-seeds (*vipāka-bīja*) that cause consciousness to maintain the body, abide, and exercise appropriation (*upādāna*).
The first type is established based on the similar states of matter and mind;
this refers to the "homogeneity of beings" (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

It is a provisional designation established according to the specific categories of sentient beings within the five destinies of humans, gods, and so forth, as they share no distinction among their respective types.
The five [categories] are established based on the states of the flow of matter and mind;
that is to say, they are the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

These are provisionally established because they indicate that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) which previously did not exist now come into being, and having existed, cease to be, and so forth.
The six [factors] are established based on the states of speech regarding form and mind;
these are names (nāma), phrases (pada), and phonemes (vyañjana).
They are conventionally designated as such because they depend upon form and mind to express phenomena through the modulation of vocal sounds.
Seven [factors] are established solely in dependence on the mind and cannot be established through distinct states;
that is to say, the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
This is because it is a provisional designation based on the seeds of the afflictions of view, which prevent the mind and mental factors from becoming noble dharmas.
The ten [categories], such as "evolution" (pravṛtti) and so forth, are established based on the causal and resultant states of form and mind.
This is because these various characteristics are provisionally designated in accordance with those states by virtue of the power of cause and effect.
It should be understood that four [of these] are established based solely on the mind,
while twenty are conventionally designated based on both matter and mind;
for this reason, they also pertain to both the stages of ordinary beings and those of the noble ones.
Therefore, as stated in the sūtras cited by the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"The *pudgala* accomplishes good and evil;
the noble one accomplishes the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*)."
Furthermore, it is said:
ordinary beings do not possess the noble dharmas,
and all arhats do not possess afflictions.
The mention of "attainment" and "non-attainment" reveals that it is indeed non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
It is also said to be included within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the noble ones,
because the noble ones attain this cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Since dharmas such as cause and effect pertain to both ordinary beings and noble ones,
they are all subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha);
this is because it is taught that these are all dissociated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
These are also subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*),
because all other [factors] not included elsewhere are subsumed herein.
The meanings of the other categories should be reflected upon according to reason.
Treatise:
Fifth, the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are briefly of six kinds. The commentary says:
Next follows the fifth section, the "Gate Revealed by the Four."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general statement enumerating the number;
second, a detailed classification according to that number.
This is the first point.
Regarding the term "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), there are two meanings:
first, it is that which is not produced by karma or afflictions.
Second, because arising, abiding, and so forth do not involve transition or movement.
If the latter meaning exists, the former meaning must necessarily be present;
however, if the former meaning exists, the latter may be absent.
If both meanings were absent, there would be only the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
if both meanings were present, it would be designated solely as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If only the first meaning were present, the unconditioned would be fully established.
Based on this, one should formulate a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First: that which is exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The second is exclusively unconditioned,
namely the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
The third possesses both meanings.
That is, the various noble paths;
four are neither; and two are both—that is, the untainted aggregates.
Now, these six kinds are truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
for they are the true, eternal dharmas that are neither born nor extinguished. Therefore,
the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
If a phenomenon undergoes arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing,
it can be known as having the characteristic of being conditioned;
that which is contrary to the conditioned is the meaning of the unconditioned.
The "six unconditioned phenomena" (*ṣaḍ asaṃskṛtāni*) is an explanation based on enumeration.
However, regarding the number of unconditioned phenomena, there are differences in the explanations found in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, ranging from three to eight.
If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna:
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, there are three kinds:
namely, space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
All of these possess a substantial nature distinct from form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
If the Sautrāntikas and others assert that these three or nine [categories] are all not substantially existent,
I shall not set them forth here for fear of prolixity.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, [the stages] range from three to eight, differing in number.
If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it also establishes three kinds:
the first is called Nirvāṇa.
The second is space;
the third is cessation not through the condition of wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one follows the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, there are four unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
These are what are called space, cessation through deliberation, cessation not through deliberation, and the nature of suchness (tathatā).
Together with consciousness-only, these are said to be the six unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
The names for space and the others are as follows:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* establishes eight unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
further dividing true suchness (*tathatā*) into three types based on the distinctions between the wholesome,
the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The reason why these Dharma teachings differ in this way is that,
while the principle takes non-action as its essence and thus has neither breadth nor narrowness,
they are manifested through various distinctions of expansion and brevity, or opening and closing.
To manifest the comprehensive exposition that explains both the general and the specific,
the *Xiányáng lùn* (Exposition of Manifestation) opens this into eight kinds;
for the three natures and suchness do not possess separate entities.
Because they are combined into one, six types are taught.
Regarding the immobility of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-aniñjya*), there are two meanings:
if it is merely temporarily suppressed, it is subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If they are permanently destroyed, they are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because they are explained according to four distinct meanings, they are divided into six;
because they are combined according to their suppression and illumination, they are condensed into four.
Although the four meanings differ due to distinctions in their essential natures (*svabhāva*),
they all possess the nature of nirvāṇa and thus comprise three types.
By this, all the various teachings are mutually non-contradictory.

Treatise: First, space; second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); third, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); fourth, the imperturbable (*āniñjya*); fifth, the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*); sixth, suchness (*tathatā*). The Commentary states:
This is an enumeration based on the teachings for the sake of clarification.
These six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not fully accounted for within the Vijñaptimātra system.
Now, citing various treatises, they are collectively explained as follows:
Regarding what is called "space" (*ākāśa*):
Regarding the meaning of non-obstruction:
in the Hīnayāna, this is manifested solely in relation to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
Space has non-obstruction as its sole nature;
because it is unobstructed, matter moves within it.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* are largely identical to the *Abhidharmakośa* on this point.
In the Mahāyāna, it is generally taught that the five aggregates are non-existent;
thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* state:
"The five aggregates are nowhere spoken of as being [other than] space."
It is called "void" (*khya*) because it cannot obstruct objects;
it is described as "empty" (*śūnya*) because it lacks form and other such qualities.
"Void" is itself "empty"; this is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (appositional compound).
Regarding what is called "analytical cessation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
it has the meaning of dissociation (visamyoga).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*);
cessation (*nirodha*) is its fruit.
Because it is a cessation obtained through discernment, it is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
In this context, there are two kinds of the fruit of cessation (*nirodha-phala*): first, that which results from the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"That which is the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is so called because it permanently eradicates the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)."
The *Pañcaskandhaka-prakaraṇa* states:
"Due to the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*), the aggregates (*skandha*) ultimately do not arise.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
The arising of all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) is ultimately ceased.
This is demonstrated by reasoning;
thus, it is stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
It is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because it is the ultimate realization that extinguishes all afflictions;
it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the cessation [attained] by means of discernment.
As for "non-discernment cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):
It does not have the meaning of dissociation (*visamyoga*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"That which is not attained through the wisdom of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
It is not because it selects a fruit;
this non-selection of a fruit also has two meanings.
First, the afflictions do not arise of their own accord.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"This is not a disjunction [from defilements], because it does not permanently destroy the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
The permanent destruction of future arising that occurs without depending on analytical discernment,
but rather by virtue of the absence of conditions, is called "cessation not through discernment" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The nature of these two [cessations] is self-evident.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"It is intrinsically pure by virtue of its own nature, not through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
