This refers to the analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
That which is called "immovable" has the meaning of being unchanging.
It subsumes the three types of sensation and divides them into two kinds.
The two sensations of suffering and pleasure are termed "transformation.
Noble ones (ārya) attain the fourth dhyāna by severing these seeds through the untainted (anāsrava) path.
Because they have severed them, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state is attained, wherein suffering and pleasure no longer arise.
It is named "Immovable.
Although one may partially attain this concentration during the first dhyāna,
it is not established as such because it has not been perfected.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"It refers to the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) where desire for the lower realms has been abandoned, but desire for the higher realms has not yet been abandoned, and suffering and pleasure have ceased.
The two characters "immovable" (*āneñjya*) do not constitute a *ṣaṣṭhī-vigraha* (genitive compound).
As it is said, because there is no greed and no separation or union,
the cessation of perception and feeling is precisely the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
By means of observing the untainted (*anāsrava*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one enters [this state];
having thus entered, because this untainted observation does not cease or undergo transformation, the ideation and sensation previously attained are relinquished and do not function;
this is called the cessation of ideation and sensation (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Because one has abandoned desire for the third [dhyāna] and nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*),
preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of cessation (*nirodhasaṃjñā*)."

It is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) obtained through the cessation of those mental states and mental factors that do not function constantly, as well as a portion of those that do function constantly;
it is so called because this unconditioned state is attained through the cessation of perception and feeling.
Cessation belongs to perception and feeling;
when perception and feeling cease,
cessation itself belongs to the unconditioned.
Regarding the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*),
both the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analyses are applicable.
As for the term "true thusness" (*tathatā*):
It means being free from falsehood.
Regarding the term *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and so forth,
"true" (*zhen*) refers to reality (*tattva*).
As it is thus and as it always is,
it is called *tathatā* (suchness) because it is characterized by the absence of change.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
For what reason is the unconditioned called *tathatā* (suchness)?
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is without change.
"Suchness" (*tathā*) is precisely "reality" (*tā*); this is an *karmadhāraya* compound.
If these six names are applied to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
then "space" (*ākāśa*) and the others are all *karmadhāraya* compounds.
These six unconditioned phenomena are all merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Because these unconditioned phenomena possess two types of essence:
first, they are provisionally established based on the transformations of consciousness,
meaning that one has previously heard the names "space" and so forth being spoken.
Due to the power of repeated habituation to the signs of space and so forth as they are conceptually discriminated,
when the mind and its associates arise, they manifest in the likeness of unconditioned phenomena such as space.
These manifested signs remain similar from one moment to the next, without undergoing any change.
It is conventionally designated as permanent;
because it resembles that which is permanent, it is established as having the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Second, it is provisionally established based upon the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This refers to the true suchness (tathatā) manifested by emptiness and selflessness;
it transcends both existence and non-existence, is beyond the path of mind and speech,
and is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena.
Because it is the principle of these phenomena, it is called the "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).
Because it is free from all obstructions, it is called "space" (ākāśa).
Because it severs obstructions and realizes realization, it is called "analytical cessation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Intrinsic purity is termed non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The cessation of painful and pleasant feelings is termed the imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
The non-occurrence of perception and feeling is termed the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).
Suchness (*tathatā*) is also a designation established by convention.
It is said to "exist" in order to preclude its denial as non-existent;
it is said to be "empty" in order to preclude the grasping of it as existent.
Do not speak of what is illusory as being real.
Because its principle is not a false analogy, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Therefore, all six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are merely provisionally existent.
Because the true suchness apart from the mind cannot be apprehended;
if it were based on the transformation of consciousness, there could be a separate entity,
which would then perfume seeds and subsequently give rise to appearances.
If, according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), all things are merely provisional designations,
because they are established based on the principles and meanings of that nature;
and if those which are transformations of consciousness are all dependently originated (paratantra).
Because the manifested images arise from causes,
those established in dependence upon the ultimate (pariniṣpanna) are all the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva),
since they are explained according to the meaning of suchness (tathatā).
Apart from this, all other explanations are considered to be based on false attachment,
as they involve the four types of denial, such as existence and non-existence.
If that which is transformed by consciousness can be categorized across the three natures, [then it is not exclusively imagined].
Because it arises as a transformation of the mind according to the three natures,
that which is established based on the True [Nature] conforms to being of a wholesome nature,
since the True [Nature] is exclusively a pure and wholesome nature.
That which is transformed by consciousness may be said to be pervasive,
because it relies on the unimpeded characteristics of the various material entities.
That which is established based on the ultimate reality (tathatā) is neither pervasive nor non-pervasive.
Because it is unobstructed both pervasively and non-pervasively.
Its non-inclusion within the five aggregates is because it is not a phenomenon characterized by aggregation or accumulation.
As for its inclusion within the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmāyatana*,
it is because it possesses the sense of being a source of growth and a lineage;
furthermore, other meanings should be reflected upon according to reason.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement "there is no self," there are briefly two kinds. [The Master] Kai says:
The meaning of "all phenomena" has already been explained above.
Next, the second section below clarifies the absence of self (*anātman*).
This contains two parts:
first, a general presentation stating the number [of points].
This is the first [point] among those subsequently enumerated and categorized.
If one follows the Hīnayāna school, they clarify a single non-self.
Because all phenomena are grasped as being real,
whereas the person (*pudgala*) and the self (*ātman*) do not exist; thus,
the Mahāyāna school now elucidates the two kinds of selflessness.
Because all phenomena arise from conditions,
there is no separate agent apart from them;
since there is no distinct characteristic of a self apart from these phenomena.
The mark of a self as a person (pudgala) does not exist.
It is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva),
for they are impermanent from moment to moment and are not autonomous.
Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise not a real self,
they are said to be "selfless" (*anātman*).
However, if one were to follow the sūtras that speak of four types of selflessness:
This refers to the absence of a self, a person, a sentient being, or an experiencer.
The Vajra-utterer taught the eight types of non-self:

namely, a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-principle (*jīva*), a spirit (*puruṣa*), a person (*pudgala*), a mind-born (*manuja*), a youth (*mānava*), an agent (*kartṛ*), and an experiencer (*vedaka*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of thirteen kinds [of selflessness].
To the previous eight, it further adds the non-existence of a creator, a nourisher, a knower, and a perceiver;
all of these are based upon the aforementioned [doctrine of] selflessness.
That which is taught in that sūtra— that the characteristics of non-existent phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) up to and including awakening (*bodhi*) are all unattainable—
is precisely the meaning of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) within this context. Thus,
the similarities and differences among various teachings do not contradict one another.
The Treatise states:
First is the selflessness of the person (pudgala-nairātmya); second is the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya).
[Vasubandhu] says:
This is a classification according to number.
These two types of selflessness are fully elucidated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*;
I shall briefly cite passages from that treatise to explain them.
However, the absence of self (*anātman*) is established in opposition to the characteristic of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*).
Since the grasped self possesses two characteristics,
the absence of self is said to have these two names.
One should first distinguish the two types of self-characteristics.
Regarding *pudgala*, this is translated in two ways:
if translated according to worldly convention, it is called a "person" (*ren*).
Following the terminology of the translated scriptures, the term *pudgala* (person) was adopted;
thus, there is this distinction between the old and new translations.
"Dharma" carries the meaning of that which serves as a norm (*viniyoga*) and that which maintains its own nature (*dhāraṇa*).
The term "self" (ātman) is designated as "sovereign.
It is called "sovereign" because it possesses the power of autonomous severance.
Non-Buddhists may instead cling to the notion that all phenomena possess distinct, substantial realities.
"I am the agent" refers to the mark of a self as a *pudgala*.
Ordinary worldlings may further cling to the notion that the aggregates, such as form and so forth, all possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
These, such as "that which can produce" and so forth,
are precisely the characteristics of the selfhood of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) within this context.
Now, in the Buddha-dharma, it is revealed that such characteristics of a self do not exist.
Therefore, it is here that the two kinds of selflessness are revealed.
If there were a separate, substantial self apart from all phenomena,
then all phenomena would necessarily be substantially permanent.
Because an agent is devoid of transformation or cessation,
the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Apart from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced through dependent origination, no separate, substantial self (*ātman*) can be found."
If the very dharmas were designated as the self,
then all dharmas would not be impermanent,
because they would possess the characteristics of a sovereign, real self.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arising through dependent origination are by nature not a real self, because they are impermanent.
Thus, this refers to the meaning of the two kinds of selflessness: that of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and that of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
This is explained in detail in works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Herein, both persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) are termed "selfless" (*anātman*),
which is precisely in contrast to the discourses on the characteristics of selfhood regarding both persons and phenomena.
In the Vijñaptimātra system, however, the self and phenomena are distinct:
the various aspects of the self are designated as the sentient being, the life-principle, and so forth;
the various aspects of phenomena are designated as the aggregates, bases, and elements, and so forth.
This is based on the actual meaning;
that [designation] is applied by way of the predominance of characteristics,

It is by focusing exclusively on sentient beings that its characteristic of selfhood is revealed;
therefore, the principles of the two kinds of emptiness differ regarding both self and phenomena.
This is so even if one clings to the notion of a truly existent, autonomous, and eternal [self].
Thus, the meaning of "self" (ātman) also applies to all phenomena (dharmas).
Therefore, non-self (anātman) applies to both persons (pudgala) and phenomena.
If this is so, why are there two types of grasping (grāha)?
Is the mark of self taught in this holy teaching?
Answer:
It is taught as a provisional designation based on the habitual perfuming of delusion.
This means that because all sentient beings have been habituated by the power of beginningless false clinging to a real self,
when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as the semblance of a self.
Although these two aspects of the self exist within internal consciousness, [they appear as external].
Rather, it arises from conceptual construction as if it were an external object,
like a magical illusion or a dream;
by the power of such illusions and dreams, the mind appears in the form of various external objects.
Based on this, one grasps it as a real self-characteristic.
Each of these two types of self-characteristic has two kinds:
first, the innate; second, the acquired.
The second is the conceptual [form of] innate self-grasping;
due to the internal causal power of false habitual perfuming since beginningless time,
it is ever present together with the body.
Because it arises spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false discrimination,
it is called "innate" (*sahaja*).
This, moreover, is of two kinds.
First, it is constantly continuous:
residing in the seventh consciousness, it takes the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to the manifestation of its own mind, grasping it as a real self.
Second, it is intermittent.
When the sixth consciousness takes as its object the appearances of the five appropriated aggregates (pañcopādānaskandha) transformed by consciousness—
whether collectively or individually— it gives rise to the grasping of its own mental images as a real self.
Because these two types of self-grasping are subtle, they are difficult to sever.
Only through the repeated cultivation of the two superior types of emptiness-contemplation within the subsequent path of cultivation can the conceptual grasping at a self be eliminated; furthermore,
because it arises through the power of present external conditions, it does not coexist with the body.
It is called "discrimination" because it only arises after depending upon false teachings and false conceptualization;
it exists solely within the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness.
This, moreover, is of two kinds.
First, based on the characteristics of the aggregates as taught by false teachings, one gives rise to mental images within one's own mind,
which are then conceptually imputed and grasped as a real self.
Second, based on the characteristics of a self, a self-nature, and so forth as taught by false teachings, one gives rise to mental images within one's own mind.
One discriminates and calculates, grasping at them as a real self.
These two types of self-grasping are coarse and thus easy to sever;
upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one contemplates all phenomena.
The suchness of the two kinds of emptiness can eliminate these two aforementioned types of self-characteristics;
whether external phenomena exist apart from one's own mind or do not exist is thus resolved.
All phenomena within one's own mind exist;
therefore, both types of grasping take the semblance of phenomena manifested from one's own mind as the mark of a self.
Apart from what is manifested by one's own mind, they cannot be found in reality.
Both persons and dharmas are devoid of self;
the meaning of the two selves—of persons and of dharmas—is indeed boundless.
